substantial (about 2.5 MB per update). Since data transmission cost is
considered one of the main challenges in FL, our observation highlights the

-trial C-band 72Gbit/s optical on-off keying
(OOK) system over 18.8km dispersion-uncompensated submarine optical cable in
the South China Sea. Chromatic dispersion (CD) of 18.8km submarine optical
cable causes four spectral nulls on the 36GHz bandwidth of 72Gbit/s OOK signal,
which is the main obstacle for achieving an acceptable bit-error-rate (BER)
performance. Decision feedback equalizer (DFE) is effective to compensate for
the spectral nulls. However, DFE has a serious defect of burst-error
propagation when the burst errors emerge due to the unstable submarine
environment. Weighted DFE (WDFE) can be used to mitigate the burst-error
propagation, but it cannot fully compensate for the spectral nulls because only
a part of feedback symbols is directly decided. Fortunately, maximum likelihood
sequence estimation (MLSE) can be added after the WDFE to simultaneously
eliminate the resisting spectral distortions and implement optimal detection.
Compared to the joint DFE and MLSE algorithm, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm
can effectively suppress the burst-error propagation to obtain a maximum 2.9dB
improvement of $\boldsymbol{Q}$ factor and eliminate the phenomenon of BER
floor. In conclusion, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm can effectively
compensate for the spectral nulls to obtain a BER less than 10$^{-3}$. Therefore,
this joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm is suitable for the CD optical communication
systems with unstable sources.

handling inconsistencies in tables
with missing values (also called nulls) and functional dependencies. Although
the traditional view is that table instances must respect all functional
dependencies imposed on them, it is nevertheless relevant to develop theories
about how to handle instances that violate some dependencies. Regarding missing
values, we make no assumptions on their existence: a missing value exists only
if it is inferred from the functional dependencies of the table.
  We propose a formal framework in which each tuple of a table is associated
with a truth value among the following: true, false, inconsistent or unknown;
and we show that our framework can be used to study important problems such as
consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality measures - to
mention just a few. In this paper, however, we focus mainly on consistent query
answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last
decades.
  The main contributions of the paper are the following: (a) we introduce a new
approach to handle inconsistencies in a table with nulls and functional
dependencies, (b) we give algorithms for computing all true, inconsistent and
false tuples, (c) we investigate the relationship between our approach and
Four-valued logic in the context of data merging, and (d) we give a novel
solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to
that of table repairs.
  We believe that our framework provides a number of opportunities for further
research, especially with respect to data quality measures, table merging, and
consistent query answering.

Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2) using high-resolution near-infrared spectra collected
with the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II survey
(APOGEE-2), obtained as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. We investigate
chemical abundances for a variety of species including the light-, odd-Z,
$\alpha$-, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements from high S/N spectra of seven
giant members. The derived mean cluster metallicity is [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$,
with no evidence for an intrinsic metallicity spread. Ton~2 exhibits a typical
$\alpha$-enrichment that follows the trend for high-metallicity Galactic GCs,
similar to that seen in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. We find a significant nitrogen
spread ($>0.87$ dex), and a large fraction of nitrogen-enriched stars that
populate the cluster. Given the relatively high-metallicity of Ton~2, these
nitrogen-enriched stars are well above the typical Galactic levels, indicating
the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon in this cluster which also
contains several stars with typical low, first-generation N abundances. We also
identify the presence of [Ce/Fe] $\geq$ 0.50 in three cluster stars, which is
high compared to other GCs. Lastly, we report the presence of the rare
strontium II $^3$D$_{1}$-$^3$D$_{2}$ line at 5218.80 nm in two cluster stars,
and carefully derive an overall cluster Sr abundance pattern. Ton~2 exhibits a
marginally elevated [Sr/O] $\sim$ 0.50, which could indicate the presence of at
least one generation of r-process-enriched material. We discuss the origin of
the complex chemical picture in Ton~2, which appears to have experienced multiple
star formation episodes with different chemical signatures.
  Finally, we point out that the multiple-population phenomenon in this relatively
high-metallicity GC highlights the role of primordial or early-fossil CN cycle
sources, likely resulting from the evolution of massive stars.
  We demonstrate that the N enrichment in the stars of Ton~2 can be explained in
terms of the simple contribution of multiple sources

technology. A metasurface is a complex electromagnetic structure, that is
typically deeply subwavelength in thickness, electrically large in transverse
size and composed of subwavelength scattering particles with extremely small
features; it may generally be bianisotropic, spacevarying and time-varying,
nonlinear, curved and multiphysics. With such complexity, the design of a
metasurface requires a holistic approach, involving synergistic synthesis and
analysis operations, based on a solid model. The Generalized Sheet Transition
Conditions (GSTCs), combined with bianisotropic surface susceptibility
functions, provide such a model, and allow now for the design of sophisticated
metasurfaces, which still represented a major challenge a couple of years ago.
This paper presents this problematic, focusing on the computational analysis of
metasurfaces via the GSTC-susceptibility approach. It shows that this analysis
plays a crucial role in the holistic design of metasurfaces, and overviews
recently reported related frequency-domain (FDFD, SD-IE, FEM) and time-domain
(FDTD) computational techniques.
  Although not exhaustively, this overview highlights again the interest of
using physics-based computational techniques, and more specifically those based
on solving the Maxwell's equations, to analyze and design various types of
metasuraces. It emphasizes that the successful design of such structures
requires a thorough understanding of their electromagnetic response,
information that can be solely provided by electromagnetic modeling techniques.
Finally, it highlights that future modeling tasks arise with the growing
interest for multiphysics metasurfaces, i.e. structures embedding functional
layers for other physical phenomena than electromagnetism.

  Let $r\geq 2$ be an integer, $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_r\in C^{\infty}(M)$ be

field $X$ is said to be formally-equivalent to a linear vector field if it

this paper is to prove that if $X$ is formally-equivalent to a linear vector
field then it is locally orbitally linearizable in the smooth category.
Moreover, the fields of tangency of the 1-form $\delta_i dx-X^{-1}(dx)$,
$i=1,dots,r$, are stable under smooth map approximations and blow-ups.

of a `Giant Arc on the Sky' at $z \sim
0.8$. The Giant Arc (GA) spans $\sim 1$ Gpc (proper size, present epoch), and
appears to be almost symmetrical on the sky. It was discovered via intervening
MgII absorbers in the spectra of background quasars, using the catalogues of
Zhu \& M\'enard. The use of MgII absorbers represents a new approach to the
investigation of large-scale structures (LSSs) at redshifts $0.45 \lesssim z
\lesssim 2.25$. We present the observational properties of the GA, and we
assess it statistically using methods based on: (i) single-linkage hierarchical
clustering ($\sim 4.5\sigma$); (ii) the Cuzick-Edwards test ($\sim 3.0\sigma$);
and (iii) power spectrum analysis ($\sim 4.8\sigma$). Each of these methods has
distinctive attributes and powers, and we advise considering the evidence from
the ensemble. We discuss our approaches to mitigating any {\it post-hoc}
aspects of analysing significance after discovery. The overdensity of the GA is
$\delta \rho / \rho \sim 1.3 \pm 0.2$. The region contains at least 8 CIII* emitters
and contains the `Cosmic String' reported by a previous analysis. Follow-up
imaging with the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) on Hubble has yielded 3
bright ( $m \gtrsim 24$ ) sources within the GA, and these may represent the
tips of the giant arc's "cosmic spikes". Future observations with the Legacy
Integrating Spectograph and Exploration Spectograph on James Webb Space Telescope
(JWST) will allow these CIII* emitters to be spatially resolved, enabling a
comprehensive investigation of the GA's physical scale and orientation.
Additionally, the Multi-Object Spectryo-graph (MOSAIC) instrument on the Next
Generation Space Telescope (NGST) will allow the CIII* emitters to be
spatially resolved and will be ideally suited to further exploiting the rich
pickings within the GA. We discuss the potential for the GA to be a "cosmic
thread" linking several separate structures.

D pose of object instances with
convolutional neural network (CNN) has received considerable attention.
Depending on whether intermediate cues are used, the relevant literature can be
roughly divided into two broad categories: direct methods and two stage
pipelines. For the latter, intermediate cues, such as 3D object coordinates,
semantic keypoints, or virtual control points instead of pose parameters are
regressed by CNN in the first stage. Object pose can then be solved by
correspondence constraints constructed with these intermediate cues. In this
paper, we focus on the postprocessing of a two-stage pipeline and propose to
combine two learning concepts for estimating object pose under challenging
scenes: projection grouping on one side, and correspondence learning on the
other. We firstly employ a local patch based method to predict projection
heatmaps which denote the confidence distribution of projection of 3D bounding
box's corners. A projection grouping module is then proposed to remove
redundant local maxima from each layer of heatmaps. Instead of directly feeding
2D-3D correspondences to the perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm, multiple
correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and its corresponding
neighborhood and ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally,
correspondences with higher confidence are selected to determine object pose.
Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that the proposed
framework outperforms several state-of-the-art methods.

package for solving General Graphical Lasso
problems. The Graphical Lasso scheme, introduced by (Friedman 2007) (see also
(Yuan 2007; Banerjee 2008)), estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix
$\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,
\Sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^p$. Originally proposed by (Dempster 1972) under the
name Covariance Selection, this estimation framework has been extended to
include latent variables in (Chandrasekaran 2012). Recent extensions also
include the joint estimation of multiple inverse covariance matrices, see,
e.g., in (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package contains methods for
solving a general problem formulation, including important special cases, such
as, the single (latent variable) Graphical Lasso, the Group, and the Fused
Graphical Lasso.
  GGLasso provides an easy-to-use interface allowing developers to express
problems in a natural way, working with a wide range of indeterminacies, and
computing estimates together with associated consistency diagnostics. In
addition, GGLasso provides a graphical user interface (GUI) allowing users to
load data, select appropriate estimation parameters and view the resulting
estimation graphically.
  GGLasso is written in Python, making extensive use of NumPy and SciPy. It
contains interfaces to the high-performance Lasso solver 'ospal' and the GUI

with their environments can be
studied using numerical relativity simulations. These start only a short finite
time before merger, at which point appropriate initial conditions must be
imposed. A key task is therefore to identify the configuration that is
appropriate for the binary and its environment at this stage of the evolution.
In this work we study the behaviour of wave dark matter around equal mass black
hole binaries, finding that there is a preferred, quasi-stationary profile that
persists and grows over multiple orbits, in contrast to heavier mass dark
matter where any overdensity tends to be dispersed by the binary motion. Whilst
different initial configurations converge to the preferred quasi-stationary one
after several orbits, unwanted transient oscillations are generated in the
process, which may impact on the signal in short simulation runs. We also point
out that naively superimposing the matter onto a circular binary results in
artificially eccentric orbits due to the matter backreaction, which is an
effect of the initial conditions and not a signature of dark matter. We discuss
the further work required so that comparison of waveforms obtained with
environments to vacuum cases can be done in a meaningful way.

pattern when viewed from the binary perspective, which may be used as a
highly efficient starting configuration, reducing to <1% of the time it takes
to reach merger for the simulations presented here. Using this starting
configuration, we have obtained waveforms for 9 different pairs of black hole
masses, including equal mass binaries. We further show that by requiring that
the matter is in the quasi-stationary phase, the need for multiple orbits for
convergence of simulation results is greatly reduced. And finally, we discuss
how this starting configuration can be analytically derived using the

  We propose a new mathematical model of an electric motor, which is suited
for inverse problems like the discrimination between a genuine motor and a
remote control of an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). Based on the two-current
vectorial model for UAVs, we introduce an electric circuit describing the
operation of the imagined motor. With regard to discrimination tasks, this
model has the advantage over existing approaches that it produces a range of
distinct states, which can be better exploited in inverse problems than the
gradual switching functions assumed in the existing literature. We focus on a
discrimination problem, where we are given measurements of the electromagnetic
properties of a UAV equipped with an unknown electric motor and aim to
determine whether it is a remote control equipped with a standard electric
motor or a vehicle equipped with a proposed model of an electric motor. We
solve this problem explicitly by observing the harmonic magnetic field around
the UAV and exploiting the fact that the proposed model of the electric motor
has a number of distinct operating modes. In the case of a single observation
from a fixed viewpoint, we provide a decision rule which is correct for all

variant of eigenvector centrality
for multilayer networks with inter-layer constraints on node importance.
Specifically, we consider a multilayer network defined by multiple
edge-weighted, potentially directed, graphs over the same set of nodes with
each graph representing one layer of the network and no inter-layer edges. As
in the standard eigenvector centrality construction, the importance of each
node in a given layer is based on the weighted sum of the importance of
adjacent nodes in that same layer. Unlike standard eigenvector centrality, we
assume that the adjacency relationship and the importance of adjacent nodes may
be based on distinct layers. Importantly, this type of centrality constraint is
only partially supported by existing frameworks for multilayer eigenvector
centrality that use edges between nodes in different layers to capture
inter-layer dependencies. For our model, constrained, layer-specific
eigenvector centrality values are defined by a system of independent eigenvalue
problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, whose solution can be
efficiently realized using an interleaved power iteration algorithm.
Furthermore, our approach is broadly applicable to a variety of network models,
is flexible in terms of the type of layers a network may have, and is able to
capture a variety of different types of constrained eigenvector centrality that
have been previously reported in the literature. Finally, we show that our
approach is naturally embedded into a multiple pseudo-eigenvector procedure that
allows us to tackle a variety of general node influence problems.
  We study the convergence properties of the proposed algorithm and establish
convergence results for both the standard and constrained power iteration. We
report a case study on a multilingual document network with layers representing
different languages and document types. Finally, we study the sensitivity of the
constrained eigenvector centrality scores to the number of references and the
influence of the structure of the network on the constrained eigenvector
centrality using a study on a multilingual bibliographic-citation network with
layers representing different languages and distinct types of citations.

ophageal tumor in CT images is known
to be very challenging. This is due to the low contrast between the tumor and
adjacent tissues, the anatomical variation of the esophagus, as well as the
occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians
therefore usually exploit additional knowledge such as endoscopic findings,
clinical history, additional imaging modalities like PET scans. Achieving his
additional information is time-consuming, while the results are error-prone and
might lead to non-deterministic results. In this paper we aim to investigate if
and to what extent a simplified clinical workflow based on CT alone, allows one
to automatically segment the esophageal tumor with sufficient quality. For this
purpose, we present a fully automatic end-to-end esophageal tumor segmentation
method based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed network,
called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), leverages spatial and channel
attention gates in each dense block to selectively concentrate on determinant
feature maps and regions. Dilated convolutional layers are used to manage GPU
memory and increase the network receptive field. We collected a dataset of 792
scans from 288 distinct patients including varying anatomies with \mbox{air
pockets}, feeding tubes and proximal tumors. Repeatability and reproducibility
studies were conducted for three distinct CT scanning protocols. Segmentation
evaluations were performed on 792 scans using various evaluation metrics. The
proposed DDAUnet achieves a Dice score of $0.873 \pm {0.001}$ and mean absolute
surface distance of $1.113 \pm {0.004}$ in a completely automatic setting.
Repeatability and reproducibility studies reveal that the proposed method
produces similar segmentation results, despite variations in patient anatomy
and scanning protocols.

segmentation? To answer this question, we present a series of ablation
experiments. The aim is to gradually build-up the network architecture,
removing one layer type at a time. It is shown that Dilated Densely-Attention
Unets outperform their counterparts, in terms of segmentation performance and
computational complexity.

and hydrocarbons are often
located in complex reservoir formations. To effectively produce from such
reservoirs and reduce costs, optimized well placement in real-time
(geosteering) is crucial. Geosteering is usually assisted by an updated
formation evaluation obtained by well-log interpretation while drilling. A
reliable, computationally efficient, and robust workflow to interpret well logs
and capture uncertainties in real-time is necessary for this application. An
iterative ensemble-based method, namely the approximate Levenberg Marquardt
form of the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML) is integrated in
our formation evaluation workflow. We estimate model parameters, resistivity
and density in addition to boundary locations, and related uncertainties by
reducing the statistical misfit between the measurements from the well logging
tools and the theoretical measurements from the forward tool simulators. The
results of analyzing several synthetic cases with several types of logs
verified that the proposed method can give good estimate of model parameters.
  By comparing the CPU time, we conclude that the proposed method has at least
about 10--125 times lower computational time compare to a common statistical
method, such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo. In addition, the
ensemble-based method can run in parallel on multiple CPUs. Testing the method
on a case inspired from a real field also yielded accurate formation
evaluation. Thus, the proposed method has high potential to be applied on
real-time well logging interpretation task.
  Finally, we suggest that by deploying an iterative ensemble-based method on
a high-performance computer while drilling, we can provide updated formation
evaluation and geologically meaningful uncertainties to support geosteering
decision-making.

one of core knowledge
extraction techniques, named entity recognition (NER) is widely used to extract
information from texts for downstream tasks. Nested NER is a branch of NER in
which the named entities (NEs) are nested with each other. However, most of the
previous studies on nested NER usually apply linear structure to model the
nested NEs which are actually accommodated in a hierarchical structure. Thus in
order to address this mismatch, this work models the full nested NEs in a
sentence as a holistic structure, then we propose a holistic structure parsing
algorithm to disclose the entire NEs once for all. Besides, there is no
research on applying corpus-level information to NER currently. To make up for
the loss of this information, we introduce Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI)
and other frequency features from corpus-aware statistics for even better
performance by holistic modeling from sentence-level to corpus-level.
Experiments show that our model yields promising results on widely-used
benchmarks which approach or even achieve state-of-the-art. Further empirical
studies show that our proposed corpus-aware features can substantially improve
NER domain adaptation, which demonstrates the surprising advantage of our
proposed corpus-level holistic structure modeling.

such as $\mathbb{A}^1$-enumeration with values in the Grothendieck-Witt ring,
and rationality over Henselian valued fields, using bitangents to plane
quartics as a test case. We consider quartic curves over valued fields whose
tropicalizations are smooth and satisfy a mild genericity condition. We then
express obstructions to rationality of bitangents and their points of tangency
in terms of twisting of edges of the tropicalization; the latter depends only
on the tropicalization and the initial coefficients of the defining equation
modulo squares.
  We also show that the GW-multiplicity of a tropical bitangent, i.e., the
multiplicity with which its lifts contribute to the $\mathbb{A}^1$-enumeration
of bitangents as defined by Larson and Vogt, can be computed from the
tropicalization of the quartic together with the initial coefficients of the
defining equation. As an application, we show that the four lifts of most
tropical bitangent classes contribute $2\mathbb{H}$, twice the class of the
hyperbolic plane, to the $\mathbb{A}^1$-enumeration, providing evidence for a
conjecture of Larson and Vogt on the $\mathbb{A}^1$-enumeration of bitangents.
Finally, we show that the result holds equally for bitangents to plane
sextics.
  Computation of lifts of tropical points and their points of tangency
depending on the geometry of the tropicalization and the initial coefficients
of the defining equation are key ingredients of the above results. We provide
an explicit formula for this in the case of bitangents to plane quartics.
Moreover, we provide algorithms for two such computations in the case of
bitangents to quartics and sextics, respectively, as an example of the
methodology developed in this paper.
  Finally, we show that the arithmetic tropical approach to enumerative problems
produces sharp results. For example, there exist quartics for which exactly two
of the four lifts of a tropical bitangent contribute $2\mathbb{H}$ to the
$\mathbb{A}^1$-enumeration.
  All results are expressed in terms of an explicit combinatorial
characterization of the tropicalizations of smooth quartics with rational bitangents.

  Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have numerous applications in national
security, health care and process control to name a few. Most of these
applications require the location of the members of the network to be known.
Several research efforts have been put into localizing WSNs. However, there is
little work on the co-location problem i.e. determining the relative location
of two or more sensors within a certain distance of each other. Several
applications such as seismic activities, disease spreading and multipath
interference avoidance require the resolution of this problem. In this paper we
present a novel direction of research namely, relative localization of WSNs.
We present two algorithms based on signal strength (RSS) detection to determine
when two sensors are within a certain distance of each other. These algorithms
have been implemented on the TelosB platform and have achieved an accuracy of
3cm and 1cm for algorithms A and B respectively.
  This work appears in the Proceedings of the 2009 IEEE PerCom Workshops
session on Wireless Sensor Networks Localisation, March 2009.
  Several localization algorithms have been proposed for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) based
wireless sensor networks (WSNs). However, these algorithms do not determine the
orientation of the sensors. In this paper, we present a novel beam orientation
localization algorithm based on the radio frequency (RF) signal strength
available from known locations. The algorithm is cast in a signal processing
framework and does not require cross product calculations. This is the first
localized measurement available for RF modules operating in the 2.4GHz band.
Simulation and hardware results show that the system can determine an orientation
accuracy of within 10 degrees.

previous work reported for other platforms, circulation was not mainly caused

system: misinformation news items scaled linearly with the number of users in

state-level personality and cultural factors (R2 = {0.12, 0.39}), rather than

duration and expressiveness are present along the four dimensions, highlighting

technological advancement of robot learning from demonstration methods.

across demonstrations of the same subtasks and also across different subtasks.
In contrast, other features such as semantic content of speech were found to
depend on teacher experience and written guidelines following an instruction
standard. These results underscore the importance of investigating not just
robustness to varying audio from teachers but also its utility towards specific
goals. Besides, the findings presented here can serve as a benchmark dataset

bilingual corpus as TM and employs source-side similarity search for memory

learnable memory retrieval in a cross-lingual manner. Our framework has unique
advantages. First, the cross-lingual memory retriever allows abundant
monolingual data to be TM. Second, the memory retriever and NMT model can be
jointly optimized for the ultimate translation goal. Experiments show that the
proposed method obtains substantial improvements. Remarkably, it even
outperforms strong TM-augmented NMT baselines using bilingual TM. Owning to the
ability to leverage monolingual data, our model also demonstrates effectiveness
in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios.
  Differently from previous studies on using TM for NMT, Duan et al. (2021) use
TM to enhance dialog generation. They propose a retrieval-augmentation framework
that learns to select the most relevant TM sentence to complement the context
for retrieval. Differently, our work focuses on sentence generation, namely,
retrieval instead of augmentation.
  Reproducing the result of Duan et al. (2021) is challenging because of the
following reasons. 1) The performance of the baseline generation model needs to
be high enough so that the improvement brought by TM is noticeable. We find that
the baseline model in Duan et al. (2021) achieves practically similar scores
than our baseline models. 2) The proper construction of the memory needs careful
consideration. In particular, the issue of over-repetition (e.g. generating the
same sentence multiple times) should be addressed.
  With these considerations, we propose two simple but effective methods for TM
construction. We show that they achieve noticeable improvements over the
baselines. We also study the effect of increasing the scale of monolingual data
and that of adding parallel data to the low-resource scenario.
  Finally, we study the effect of different memory representations (phrase and
subword) on generation performance. Intuitively, using phrase-level memory
should be more likely to improve translation accuracy, as phrases are units of
meaning and can be directly related to words in target language. However, our
results indicate that using subword-level memory usually yields better performance
than using phrase-level memory.

king points in the Cosmic Microwave Background
(CMB), resulting from black hole mergers and black hole evaporation,
respectively, in a previous cycle of the universe, have been predicted as
possible evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model (CCC) introduced by
R. Penrose. We present a high-resolution search for such low-variance circles
in the Planck and WMAP CMB data, and introduce HawkingNet, our machine learning
open-source software based on a ResNet18 algorithm, to search for Hawking
points in the CMB. We find that CMB anomalies, consisting of a single or a few
bright pixels, erroneously lead to regions with many low-variance circles when
applying the search criteria used in previous works [V.G. Gurzadyan, R.
Penrose]. After removing the anomalies from the data no statistically
significant low-variance circles can be found. Concerning Hawking points, also
no statistically significant evidence is found when using a Gaussian
temperature amplitude model over 1 degree opening angle and after accounting
for CMB anomalies. That CMB anomalies themselves might be remnants of Hawking
points is not supported by low-variance and/or high-temperature circles around
them. The absence of such distinct features in the CMB does not disprove CCC
because if the density of such circles and Hawking points is large an averaging
effect would be visible in the CMB, which has been verified recently through
their detection in simulated CMB data based on the WMAP resolution.
  Accordingly, the present negative results do not disprove the CCC conjecture
and further analysis of CMB data of higher resolution than WMAP is necessary to
definitively establish the non-existence of such features.

formulated as a network-based multi-agent optimization problems with equilibrium
constraints (N-MOPEC), considering the decentralized charging decisions of EV
owners and the cost-saving investment in grid infrastructure by utilities.

contains complementarity conditions. To overcome these difficulties, we propose a
novel computational algorithm based on exact convex reformulation. We conduct

allocations can lead to significant performance improvements over DRAM-only
configurations. With streaming applications, Optane DC PMMs can improve

grids can lead to higher memory traffic than necessary if the data is stored in

consumption.

persistent memory datasets, and we anticipate that this class of software will

In this paper, we consider the multi-agent extension of the Motivation Dynamics
framework and show how the framework can be extended to encode persistent
multi-agent rendezvous behaviors. We analytically characterize the bifurcation
properties of the resulting system, and numerically show that it exhibits
complex recurrent behavior suggestive of a strange attractor.
  When encoding decision-making behavior in an autonomous system, it is often
desired that an agent switch between different modes of behavior in response to
a sensed cue. While the Motivation Dynamics framework has been shown to be
capable of encoding such switch-like behavior analytically, the resulting
dynamics are often fixed-point or limit-cycle attractors, which run for only a
short time before switching to the next mode. In this paper, we use a
four-state Motivation Dynamics model to encode a sequence of prey-like modes of
behavior which gradually change from attracting slowly to attracting quickly as
a cue is sensed. We show that the resulting dynamics exhibit a gradual
acceleration and deceleration consistent with the sensed cue, and discuss the
results in the context of insect locomotion.
  Recent work has introduced the Motivation Dynamics framework for encoding
decision-making behavior in an autonomous mobile agent. This framework provides
a high-level interface for designing and testing the functionality of
autonomous systems, and could be particularly useful in the context of
human-robot interaction, in which the system should perform in a predictable
way that corresponds to its sensed intentions and goals. However, the
Motivation Dynamics framework has only been implemented in simulation so far.
We introduce an implementation of the framework on a dual-core, wireless
autonomous mobile platform called Naro. We show that the mobile platform
accurately tracks the analytically predicted bifurcation behavior, and
demonstrate how the platform can be used to design and test a simple
navigation system that incorporates multiple modes of decision-making behavior.
Finally, we show that the mobile platform can be used to evaluate the performance
of a Motivation Dynamics system by measuring it against a set of performance
metrics.

creation and control
of high-performance solid-state telecom photon-spin interfaces. T radiation
damage centres in silicon provide a promising photon-spin interface due to
their narrow O-band optical transition near 1326 nm and long-lived electron and
nuclear spin lifetimes. To date, these defect centres have only been studied as
ensembles in bulk silicon. Here, we demonstrate the reliable creation of high
concentration T centre ensembles in the 220 nm device layer of
silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers by ion implantation and subsequent annealing.

benchmark the characteristic optical spectral diffusion within these T centre
ensembles. Using this new technique, we show that with minimal optimization to
the fabrication process high densities of implanted T centres localized
$\lesssim$100 nm from an interface display ~1 GHz characteristic levels of
total spectral diffusion.

high-performance telecom photon-spin interfaces, and the future development and
application of SOI technology to boost the transition frequency of the T centre

a medical image processing technique that
used radio waves to scan the body. It is a tomographic imaging technique,
principally used in the field of radiology. With the advantage of being a
painless diagnostic procedure, MRI allows medical personnel to illustrate clear
pictures of the anatomy and the physiological processes occurring in the body,
thus allowing early detection and treatment of diseases. These images, combined
with image processing techniques may be used in the detection of tumors,
difficult to identify with the naked eye. This digital assignment surveys the
different image processing techniques used in Automated Tumor Detection (ATD).
This assignment initiates the discussion with a comparison of traditional
techniques such as Morphological Tools (MT) and Region Growing Technique (RGT).
It continues with the discussion of advanced technology used in ATD, which include
Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Semantic Segmentation (SS) and Deep
Detectors (DD). This assignment further highlights the advantages and disadvantages
of each technique as well as their applications and the next step of improvement.
Finally, this assignment concludes with a comparison of the techniques and a
recommendation on the best method for ATD.
  Deep learning methods, particularly Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) have
shown promising results against the Automated Tumor Detection (ATD) problem.
However, these models sometimes produce incorrect results when presented with
MRI images belonging to a different source. This tendency of deep learning models
to be trained on data from a specific source domain and fail to converge on
other similar domains is referred to as the problem of domain shift. This
research aims to present an approach to extend deep learning models to MRI
tumors based on varying field strength (from 1.5T to 3T) and manufacturer
(Philips to Siemens). The approach involves using a minimum number of images to
train a domain shift resistant model. The model is tested using 3T images from
two unique institutions (one using Philips equipment and the other using Siemens
equipment). The results of the test show that the model is stable and effective
in detecting tumors from 3T MRI images belonging to different institutions,
irrespective of the manufacturer of the MRI machine.

interesting algebraic, symmetric and dynamical properties that could be

properties and a randomised algorithm that samples the line combination space.

signal from other sources of noise, and on AD Leo and DS Leo to examine its
consistency at mitigating jitter for different activity levels. The analysis is
complemented with planetary injection tests. The parametric selection yields a
RV RMS reduction of less than 10%, while the randomised selection a systematic
>50% improvement, regardless of the activity level of the star examined.
Furthermore, if activity is the dominant source of noise, this approach allows

  Entity recommendation has become a crucial task in helping users discover
relevant entities on online knowledge graphs, such as Wikipedia and YAGO. While
state-of-the-art techniques often focus on web-scale static datasets, our
framework learns from Wikipedia itself as a dynamic social network layered on
top of a knowledge graph. At the foundation of this social network is the
citation graph of Wikipedia, which our entity recommendation framework organizes
complementary learning representations for by combining link analysis with
content-based techniques. Through offline and online evaluations, we show that

a major barrier in kidney
transplantation (KT). The increasing shortage of kidney donors has driven the
development of desensitization techniques to overcome this immunological
challenge. Compared with compatible KT, patients undergoing incompatible KTs
are more likely to experience rejection, infection, malignancy, and graft loss.
We study the optimal acceptance of possibly incompatible kidneys for individual
end-stage kidney disease patients. To capture the effect of incompatibility, we
propose a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model that explicitly includes
compatibility as a state variable. The resulting higher-dimensional model makes
it more challenging to analyze, but under suitable conditions, we derive
structural properties including control limit-type optimal policies that are
easy to compute and implement. Numerical examples illustrate the behavior of
the optimal policy under different mismatch levels and highlight the importance
of explicitly incorporating the incompatibility level into the acceptance
decision when desensitization therapy is an option.
  The model presented in this article can be extended to other organ transplants
and may be more generally applicable to any two-state problem with a persistent
state variable that affects the transition function. Such an extension could be
useful in guiding acceptance decisions for a wide range of transplant types.
Furthermore, the analysis presented here could be applied to derive results in
other settings with similar structural features.
  Patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) compete for a limited number of
kidney transplants (KTs). We present a Markov model that captures the
competition for KTs as a first-come-first-served process conditional on medical
admissibility. We show that the distribution of time until KT receipt follows
a recursive discrete distribution, which can be used to calculate the utility
of being on the waiting list. We derive explicit expressions for the expected
utility of being on the waiting list in time until KT receipt, until KT
receipt plus a horizon, and a discrete approximation of the expected utility
over all times until KT receipt receipt.
  We apply the model to calculate the expected utility of being on the
waiting list until KT receipt, until KT receipt plus 2 years, and a discrete
approximation of the expected utility over all times until KT receipt for
patients listed for KTs under UNOS policies without priority age and with
priority age, and compare the results, and investigate how age affects the
expected utility until KT receipt and how it affects the relative expected
utility until KT receipt under the two policies.

and predict from, particularly in high dimensions. Several algorithms to
improve the computational performance of these models are outlined. These
algorithms relate new methods for simulating from implicit copulas, compiling
an explicit probability density function for Bayesian inference, using
recurrent neural networks to represent copula densities, and exploiting the
factorization of implicit copulas to reduce the parameter burden in high
dimensions. These methods are outlined within the common auxiliary representation

techniques. Two experimental economics studies -- one from a discrete

analysis of the word2vec
model, especially when it is equipped with the Skip-gram learning scheme. Our
goal is to explain how embeddings, that are now widely used in NLP (Natural
Language Processing), are influenced by the distribution of terms in the
documents of the considered corpus. We use a mathematical formulation to shed
light on how the decision to use such a model makes implicit assumptions on the
structure of the language. We show how Markovian assumptions, that we discuss,
lead to a very clear theoretical understanding of the formation of embeddings,
and in particular the way it captures what we call frequentist synonyms. These
assumptions allow to produce generative models and to conduct an explicit
analysis of the loss function commonly used by these NLP techniques. Moreover,
we produce synthetic corpora with different levels of structure and show
empirically how the word2vec algorithm succeed, or not, to learn them. It leads
us to empirically assess the capability of such models to capture structures on
a corpus of around 42 millions of financial News covering 12 years. That for,
we rely on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists largely used on financial
texts and we show that embeddings are exposed to mixing terms with opposite
polarity, because of the way they can treat antonyms as frequentist synonyms.
Beside we study the non-stationarity of such a corpus and the evolution of
language over time.
  Let us note that our purpose is not to say word2vec is outdated, but to give
an insight on how it can be interpreted, and how one can assess its performance
on a given corpus. Depending on the considered data, other methods may
performed better, and it may be interesting to perform a similar analysis on
them.
  Finally, we hope this work will be useful to experts in NLP, and more
generally in clustering dense graphs, as we provide a clear understanding of
how such models can fail or succeed. It may lead to improve these methods and
to conduct new research in the field of analytical machine learning.
  We propose here a typology of different corpora that one can build and we
provide practitioners with questions they can answer while experimenting on
analyzing a document collection with word2vec.

currently used in computational
linguistics rely on unary modalities to allow for the controlled application of
structural rules affecting word order and phrase structure. These controlled
structural operations give rise to derivational ambiguities that are missed by
the original Lambek Calculus or its pregroup simplification. Proposals for
compositional interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed
category of FVect and linear maps have been made, but in these proposals the
syntax-semantics mapping ignores the control modalities, effectively
restricting their role to the syntax. Our aim is to turn the modalities into
first-class citizens of the vectorial interpretation. Building on the
directional density matrix semantics, we extend the interpretation of the type
system with an extra spin density matrix space. The interpretation of proofs
then results in ambiguous derivations being tensored with orthogonal spin
states. Our method introduces a way of simultaneously representing co-existing
interpretations of ambiguous utterances, and provides a uniform framework for
the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity.
  We show how the proposed interpretation preserves the proof-theoretic
properties of the syntax and how it can be applied to a range of linguistic
phenomena, including multiple utterance interpretations from a single utterance
text and the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity in interpretation
of sentences which require long-distance structural relations.
  Finally, we relate our proposal to the methodology of type-driven denotational
semantics and the approach to ambiguous interpretation as a form of quantification
over interpretations.

rationalizable behavior, where players learn to avoid iteratively dominated
actions. However, even in the basic setting of multiplayer general-sum games,
existing algorithms require a number of samples exponential in the number of
players to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper
develops the first line of efficient algorithms for learning rationalizable
Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) whose sample
complexities are polynomial in all problem parameters including the number of
players. To achieve this result, we also develop a new efficient algorithm for
the simpler task of finding one rationalizable action profile (not necessarily
an equilibrium), whose sample complexity substantially improves over the best
existing results of Wu et al. (2021). Our algorithms incorporate several novel
techniques to guarantee rationalizability and no (swap-)regret simultaneously,
including a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which
may be of independent interest. We complement our results with a sample
complexity lower bound showing the sharpness of our guarantees.
  The main idea behind our algorithms is to use a correlated exploration scheme
to boost the probability of exploring all actions uniformly. However, simply
correlating the actions to be equally likely is not enough to our tasks, as it
may not be sufficient to avoid iteratively dominated actions (CE) or delete
purely dominated actions (CCE). To address this challenge, our algorithms adapt
the correlated exploration based on the current estimation of the payoff matrix,
which ensures sufficient exploration of all actions uniformly, and thus rationalizability can be guaranteed.
  Another important aspect of our solutions is how to exploit the correlated
information to achieve polynomial sample complexities. Intuitively, the more
correlated the actions are, the higher the probability of observing the
correlated action is, and the fewer samples are needed. However, it is challenging
to guarantee the sufficient correlation of the actions since the players'
actions are determined by their individual estimates of the payoff matrix. To
address this challenge, we use the correlated exploration to boost the
correlation of the actions step-by-step. Specifically, we maintain a lower bound
on the expected correlation of the actions and use the samples to reduce this
bound. When the bound becomes smaller than a certain level, we can guarantee the
sufficient correlation of the actions and thus achieve polynomial sample
complexities.

the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ in a series of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$
superlattices as a function of bilayer thickness. Spin-lattice relaxation
measurements in an applied field of 6.55 T reveal two equal amplitude
components: one with metallic ($T$-linear) $1/T_{1}$, and a second with a more
complex $T$-dependence. The metallic character of the slow relaxing component
is only weakly affected by the LaNiO$_3$ thickness, while the fast component is
much more sensitive, exhibiting the opposite temperature dependence (increasing
towards low $T$) in the thinnest, most magnetic samples. The origin of this
bipartite relaxation is discussed.
  We propose that the fast relaxing component may be attributed to a
quantum critical point near the interface between LaNiO$_3$ and LaAlO$_3$ that
is tuned by the bilayer thickness. This hypothesis is supported by a comparison
to previous studies of single LaNiO$_3$ films and bulk LaNiO$_3$, as well as
recent studies of quantum criticality near a zero-field antiferromagnetic
transition.
  Finally, we note that the emergence of interface-driven quantum critical
behavior so far appears to be restricted to or enhanced in thin
LaNiO$_3$ layers. Further work is needed to understand the full extent of this
phenomenology and to determine if it can be tuned by external parameters.
Moreover, the origin of the zero-field quantum critical point in LaNiO$_3$ must
be disentangled before conclusions can be drawn about the underlying underlying
theory.
  Such studies could have a profound impact on our understanding of
interface-correlated quantum materials and the quantum critical points that
appear in them.

elsewhere.

$N$-body cosmological simulations in modified gravity (MG) models. We describe
the implementation, numerical tests and first results of a large suite of
cosmological simulations for three classes of MG models with conformal coupling
terms: the $f(R)$ gravity, symmetron and coupled quintessence models. Derived
from the parallel particle-mesh code GLAM, MG-GLAM incorporates an efficient
multigrid relaxation technique to solve the characteristic nonlinear partial
differential equations of these models. For $f(R)$ gravity, we have included
new variants to diversify the model behaviour, and we have tailored the
relaxation algorithms to these to maintain high computational efficiency. In a
companion paper, we describe versions of this code developed for derivative
coupling MG models, including the Vainshtein- and K-mouflage-type models.

and versatile. The code is highly optimised, with a tremendous speedup of a
factor of more than a hundred compared with earlier $N$-body codes, while still
giving accurate predictions of the matter power spectrum and dark matter halo
abundance. MG-GLAM is ideal for the generation of large numbers of MG
simulations that can be used in the construction of mock galaxy catalogues for

models result in dynamically-bound clusters at neighboring sites. We show that
the dynamics of these clusters in two-dimensional lattices is remarkably
different and richer than that of repulsively-bound on-site clusters in gases
without inter-site interactions. Whereas on-site pairs move in the same lattice
as individual particles, nearest-neighbor dimers perform an interacting quantum
walk in a different lattice geometry, leading to a peculiar dynamics
characterized by more than one time scale. The latter is general for any
lattice geometry, but it is especially relevant in triangular and diamond
lattices, where dimers move resonantly in an effective kagome and Lieb lattice,
respectively. As a result, dimers experience partial quasi-localization due to
an effective flat band, and may move slower than longer clusters. This
surprising link between anomalously slow quantum walk dynamics in these models
and flat-band physics may be readily observed in experiments with lanthanide
atoms.
  We show that three-site clusters in these models move even slower than
nearest-neighbor dimers, and propose cluster-driven interacting quantum walk
protocols in these systems. Using a weak-coupling analysis, we obtain
perturbatively large cluster dynamics in a broad range of parameters, including
both strong on-site and inter-site interactions. We find that up to 10 sites can
be bound in a single composite particle in these models.
  Our results pave the way for further investigations of dynamics of multi-site
clusters in two-dimensional extended-Hubbard and XXZ models, and related
spin-boson and spin-spin models. Such studies may lead to novel insights into
the physics of strongly-interacting gases in two-dimensional optical lattices,
and may be extended to other strongly-interacting gyromagnetic models in one and
two dimensions.
  We also propose that cluster-affected quantum walk dynamics can be studied in
continuum-wave-function experiments with bosonic or fermionic atoms. In this
regard, we show that three-site clusters can be bound in a cross-dimensional
four-body interaction, and move in an effective two-dimensional lattice.
Differences in the dynamics of dimers and three-site clusters are especially
evident in the boundary between the low-energy flat band and the higher-energy
bands.
  Finally, we note that multi-site bound states and their dynamics can be
theoretically studied in models that are not described by an effective
Hamiltonian.

reliability. To provide low latency data access, replicas are often required to
accept updates without coordination with each other, and the updates are then
propagated asynchronously. This brings the critical challenge of conflict
resolution among concurrent updates. Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT)
is a principled approach to addressing this challenge. However, existing CRDT
designs are tricky, and hard to be generalized to other data types. A design
framework is in great need to guide the systematic design of new CRDTs.
  To address this challenge, we propose RWF -- the Remove-Win design Framework
for CRDTs. RWF leverages the simple but powerful remove-win strategy to resolve
conflicting updates, and provides generic design for a variety of data
container types. Two exemplar implementations following RWF are given over the
Redis data type store, which demonstrate the effectiveness of RWF. Performance
measurements of our implementations further show the efficiency of CRDT designs
following RWF.
  In summary, RWF is a vital contribution to the CRDT community. It opens the
door for the systematic design of new CRDTs, which is of great benefit to the
development of distributed systems.

expected total population of NS LMXBs with the observed one and with the
millisecond radio pulsar (MSRP) population of the Galaxy, systems with
recurrence times well in excess of a century for outbursts detectable by
instruments like MAXI must be the dominant population of NS LMXBs, and that few
of these systems have yet been discovered.
  We therefore conclude that the argument for the presence of a large population
of stellar mass black holes in the Galactic Centre region based on the
behavior of NS LMXBs must be essentially ignored when constructing population
models for the region. We note in passing that this conclusion would also have
profound implications for the interpretation of the microlensing results from
the OGLE-IV collaboration.

systems with unusual properties, and we suggest that these are the systems
which are most likely to be caught shining as persistent sources by other

  I apply this technique to the WB sample of Hernandez et. al. (2019),

on Monte Carlo trials, the uncertainty in the one-dimensional velocity
dispersion is $\approx 100$ m/s when using sky-projected relative velocities.

less affected by distance uncertainties.
  My analysis does not support the Hernandez et. al. (2019) claim of a clear
departure from Newtonian dynamics beyond a radius of $\approx 10$ kAU, partly
because I use $2\sigma$ outlier rejection to clean their sample first.
Nonetheless, the uncertainties are small enough that existing WB data are
nearly sufficient to distinguish Newtonian dynamics from Modified Newtonian
Dynamics. I estimate that $\approx 1000$ WB systems will be required for this
purpose if using only line velocities.

systematics like undetected companions and binary evolution.

the typical system mass is large enough. I estimate that WB samples must be
pushed to $\approx 10^{-12}$ $M_{\odot$ to access the regime of interest for
small-scale MOND.

attacks: reverse multiplication attack for the logistic regression VFL

steal the private training data, even when the intermediate outputs are

complexity of the attacks is comparable to the corresponding ideal attacks (i.e.,
stealing the private training data by force). We also show that the homomorphic
encryption in some real-world VFL frameworks, such as SecureNN and

improving the security of VFL. To quantify the potential security gap, we
propose the conversion leakage model (CLM) to measure the amount of information
leaked from the encrypted intermediate outputs. Experimental results show that
the proposed measurement tool can evaluate the security of HFL and VFL, and
investigations reveal some security threats if not all) in real-world VFL

essential skill to comprehend
and reason about real world task procedures, which often requires thorough
understanding of temporal common sense and multimodal information, as these
procedures are often communicated through a combination of texts and images.
Such capability is essential for applications such as sequential task planning
and multi-source instruction summarization. While humans are capable of
reasoning about and sequencing unordered multimodal procedural instructions,
whether current machine learning models have such essential capability is still
an open question. In this work, we benchmark models' capability of reasoning
over and sequencing unordered multimodal instructions by curating datasets from
popular online instructional manuals and collecting comprehensive human
annotations. We find models not only perform significantly worse than humans
but also seem incapable of efficiently utilizing the multimodal information. To
improve machines' performance on multimodal event sequencing, we propose
sequentiality-aware pretraining techniques that exploit the sequential
alignment properties of both texts and images, resulting in > 5% significant
improvements.
  Our study further reveals that current machine learning models have a
weak understanding of structural alignment between texts and images, which
requires further investigation.
  Finally, we propose simpler and more efficient posttraining generalization
techniques that achieve additional gains.
  Experiments are conducted using popular instructional datasets such as
Instruction3D and InstructSL.

theory of percolation in networks, we analyze the phenomenon of an avalanche

fragmentation (immunization) of the network than just the single original node
removal itself. Specifically, we focus ourselves on the parameter of the size
of an avalanche, which is the number of nodes that are disconnected from the
giant component due to a single node removal. Relating to a broad range of
networks, we reveal through our research an empirical knowledge regarding the
behavior of this parameter, which is not formally proven so far. We show that
the behavior of the avalanche size parameter follows a highly skewed

of disks surrounding young stars have shown that their morphology is made of
azimuthally-symmetric or point-symmetric substructures, in some cases with
spiral arms, localized spur- or crescent-shaped features. The majority of
theoretical studies with the aim of interpreting the observational results have
focused on disk models with planets, under the assumption that the disk
substructures are due to the disk-planet interaction. However, so far only in
very few cases exoplanets have been detected in these systems. Furthermore,
some substructures are expected to appear \textit{before} planets form, as they
are necessary to drive the concentration of small solids which can lead to the
formation of planetesimals. In this work we present observational predictions
from high-resolution 3D radiative hydrodynamical models which follow the
evolution of gas and solids in a protoplanetary disk. We focus on substructures
in the distribution of millimeter-sized and smaller solid particles produced by
the vertical shear instability. We show that their characteristics are
compatible with some of the shallow gaps detected in recent observations at
sub-mm/mm wavelengths, and present predictions for future observations with
better sensitivity and angular resolution with ALMA and a Next Generation Very
Large Array.
  We predict that the vertical shear instability can explain the origin of some
of the substructures reported so far, without the need for planets. However,
our results also show that the VSI is not a powerful mechanism in disks with
outer radii smaller than a few au, and that particles larger than 1 mm are not
well trapped in the substructures if they are responsible for the 870 $\mu$m
continuum emission reported in some disks. Furthermore, the probability of
observing a sensitive ring-like feature due to the VSI is low if the disk is
too massive.
  Finally, we emphasize that the presence of sensitive shallow gaps in
observations is the signature of a population of small grains responsible for
the majority of the continuum emission in the mm/sub-mm range. These grains are
produced and sustained by the vertical shear instability in the disk gap or,
alternatively, they are produced in the disk gap but are not produced by the
VSI, e.g., by the concentration of small solids towards the mid-plane.

points of view to further investigate the role of the VSI in disk

importance of statistical models with numerous parameters. Several studies have
analyzed over-parameterized linear models with high-dimensional data that may
not be sparse; however, existing results depend on the independent setting of

time series data under over-parameterization settings. We consider an estimator

multiple dependence types. This theory can treat infinite-dimensional data
without sparsity and handle long-memory processes in a unified manner.
Moreover, we bound the risk in our theory via the integrated covariance and
nondegeneracy of autocorrelation matrices. The results show that the
convergence rate of risks with short-memory processes is identical to that of
cases with independent data, while long-memory processes slow the convergence
rate. We also present several examples of specific dependent processes that can
be applied to our setting.

of firming in low-carbon grids. A
common concern raised from ex-post assessments is that storage resources can
fail to respond to strong price signals during times of scarcity. While
commonly attributed to forecast error or failures in operations, we posit that
this behavior can be explained from the perspective of risk-averse scheduling.
Using a stochastic self-scheduling framework and real-world data harvested from
the Australian National Electricity Market, we demonstrate that risk-averse
storage resources tend to have a myopic operational perspective, that is, they
typically engage in near-term price arbitrage and chase only few extreme price
spikes and troughs, thus remaining idle in several time periods with markedly
high and low prices. This has important policy implications given the
non-transparency of unit risk aversion and apparent risk in intervention
decision-making.
  We further show that introducing prior knowledge on uncertainty can alter
risk-averse behavioral patterns, notably towards more long-term oriented
operating patterns that are less myopic. This has important implications for
ex-ante risk management and assessment of storage resources, which should not
be inferred from ex-post analyses. Finally, we compare and contrast the behavior
of storage resources introduced as simple or complex resources in the dispatch
model. We find that risk aversion leads to a form of economic complexity
efficiency, where simple resources tend to behave more efficiently than
complex resources, even when priced accordingly.
  Overall, storage resources, as the primary storage unit of analysis, are
defined as having at least one period of operational activity within a given
market day. We base our definition on the fact that most unit definitions in
the literature are technology-specific and may or may not correspond to
separate companies orco-located generators and storage resources may be combined
into a single unit. We investigate and demonstrate that costly storage resources
may fail to engage in near-term arbitrage opportunities due to risk aversion. This
paper contributes to the ongoing discussion on storage resource definition and
analysis.

of differential privacy (DP) in the
context of graph-structured data. We discuss the formulations of DP applicable
to the publication of graphs and their associated statistics as well as machine
learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks (GNNs). The
formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as
individual data points are interconnected (often non-linearly or sparsely).
This connectivity complicates the computation of individual privacy loss in
differentially private learning. The problem is exacerbated by an absence of a
single, well-established formulation of DP in graph settings. This issue
extends to the domain of GNNs, rendering private machine learning on
graph-structured data a challenging task. A lack of prior systematisation work
motivated us to study graph-based learning from a privacy perspective. In this
work, we systematise different formulations of DP on graphs, discuss challenges
and promising applications, including the GNN domain. We compare and separate
works into graph analysis tasks and graph learning tasks with GNNs. Finally, we
conclude our work with a discussion of open questions and potential directions
for further research in this area.
  We propose a new algorithm for tabular data sampling that achieves
differentially private (DP) learning while using (asymptotically) optimal
number of samples. Our method employs a graph-based data structure called a
neighborhood graph and can be used in conjunction with any private machine
learning algorithm. Our algorithm is optimal because it achieves tight bounds
on the privacy loss of any sampling algorithm for tabular data. Moreover, our
method is efficient because it uses a simple sampling procedure that does not
require learning. We show how our sampling algorithm can be used to achieve
private learning with (asymptotically) optimal performance in the sample
efficient learning setting. Finally, we show that our algorithm extends to
multi-task settings where we obtain tight privacy guarantees on feature
dimensions across multiple tasks.

simulating the otherwise difficult-to-compute dynamics of quantum many-body
systems. In this work we derive, within the positive-P phase-space formalism, a
new stochastic hydrodynamic method for the description of interacting Bose
gases. It goes beyond existing hydrodynamic approaches, such as superfluid
hydrodynamics or generalized hydrodynamics, in its capacity to simulate the
full quantum dynamics of these systems: it possesses the ability to compute
non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena.
Using this description, we derive a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme
which is able to simulate such non-equilibrium situations for longer times than
the full positive-P approach, at the expense of approximating the treatment of
quantum fluctuations, and show that this linearized scheme can be directly
connected with existing Bogoliubov approaches. Furthermore, we go on to
demonstrate the usefulness and advantages of this formalism by exploring the
correlations that arise in a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its
predictions to other established quantum many-body approaches.
  From a theoretical perspective, this work lays out a positive-P hydrodynamics
for superfluids, linking existing descriptions of equilibrium correlations and
non-equilibrium flow to a broader framework which can simulate the full
quantum dynamics of these systems. From a numerical perspective, we develop
algorithms for both the full and hydrodynamic parts of the formalism,
demonstrating their usefulness by exploring the quantum correlations in a
macroscopic quantum scenario. Lastly, we note that this work lays the groundwork
for extensions of this positive-P approach to the description of interacting
Fermi gases.

are on a collision path with other mobile robots or stationary obstacles. The

robot relative to another, guarantees reciprocal behaviour between the robots

has recently attracted a
lot of interest in wireless communications research. An IRS consists of passive
reflective elements capable of tuning the phase, amplitude, frequency and
polarization of the impinging waveforms. Given such desirable properties, the
wireless channel characteristics can be controlled and optimized for specific
signal design and processing needs -- thus promising significant potential in
radar applications. In this paper, we establish the theoretical foundations for
introducing IRS into a radar system and study the potential to improve target
parameter estimation. More specifically, we will investigate the deployment of
IRS in cases where the line-of-sight (LOS) link is weak or blocked by
obstructions. We demonstrate that the IRS can provide a virtual or
non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link between the radar and target leading to an
enhanced radar performance. The effectiveness of such an IRS-provided virtual
link in estimating the moving target parameters is illustrated under both
optimized and non-optimized IRS scenarios. Numerical simulations indicate that
the IRS can enhance the target parameter estimation when the LOS link is weaker
than $\sim 10^{-1}$ in relative strength in comparison with the NLOS link.
Furthermore, we observe that optimizing the IRS phase response can provide
additional performance enhancements, especially for larger virtual distances.
We also investigate the effect of increasing the IRS complexity and that of
increasing the number of available IRSs on the moving target parameter
estimation performance. Our results indicate that using IRS to create a virtual
or NLOS link is a promising approach to enhance radar performance, and further
research along these lines is warranted.

discover vulnerabilities in programs. Despite
considerable progress in this area in the past years, measuring and comparing
the effectiveness of fuzzers is still an open research question. In software
testing, the gold standard for evaluating test quality is mutation analysis,
assessing the ability of a test to detect synthetic bugs; if a set of tests
fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect real bugs. Mutation
analysis subsumes various coverage measures and provides a large and diverse
set of faults that can be arbitrarily hard to trigger and detect, thus
preventing the problems of saturation and overfitting. Unfortunately, the cost
of traditional mutation analysis is exorbitant for fuzzing, as mutations need
independent evaluation.
  In this paper, we apply modern mutation analysis techniques that pool
multiple mutations; allowing us, for the first time, to evaluate and compare
fuzzers with mutation analysis. We introduce an evaluation bench for fuzzers
and apply it to a number of popular fuzzers and subjects. In a comprehensive
evaluation, we show how it allows us to assess fuzzer performance and measure
the impact of improved techniques. While we find that today's fuzzers can
detect only a small percentage of mutations, this should be seen as a challenge
for future research -- notably in improving (1) detecting failures beyond
generic crashes (2) triggering mutations (and thus faults).
  Overall, mutation analysis offers a rigorous, scientifically valid methodology
for designing, evaluating, and comparing fuzzers. We hope that it will
encourage more researchers to apply it in their evaluation of fuzzer
techniques.

data and so our performance estimates are in fact stochastic, with variability
that can be substantial for natural language processing tasks. We demonstrate
that these unstable estimates cannot be relied upon for effective parameter
tuning. The resulting tuned parameters are highly sensitive to how our data is
partitioned, meaning that we often select sub-optimal parameter choices and
have serious reproducibility issues.

independent K-fold cross validations are used to assess performance. Our main
contributions are extending J-K-fold CV from performance estimation to
parameter tuning and investigating how to choose J and K. We argue that
variability is more important than bias for effective tuning and so advocate
lower choices of K than are typically seen in the NLP literature, instead use
the saved computation to increase J. To demonstrate the generality of our
recommendations we investigate a wide range of case-studies: sentiment
classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging and
document classification.

a vital role in developing NLP systems to provide confidence that the
difference in performance between two systems (i.e., the test statistic) is not
due to luck. However, practitioners rely on Monte Carlo approximation to
perform this test due to a lack of a suitable exact method. In this paper, we
develop a method for exact paired-permutation test in the context of hypothesis
testing for differences in ranking accuracy (measured by normalized discounted
cumulative gain or ndcg) using permutation. Our technique is based on Birkel's
algorithm for exact randomization test, which was previously unknown to the NLP
community. We leverage this algorithm to compute the normalized hypervolume of
the test statistic's sampling space, which allows us to compute the probability
of the observed (or more extreme) test statistics under the null hypothesis.
Since we can compute this hypervolume exactly, we can use it to speed up
Monte-Carlo approximation. Furthermore, we show that the inverse of the
hypervolume serves as a statistical significance score that is useful for
multiple-hypothesis testing. Through experiments, we show that our method is
practical and can increase the accuracy of conventional Monte-Carlo approximation.
We also propose a simple way to use the exact method to prune hypotheses that
are clearly significant or not.
  We emphasize that our contributions are not new statistical tests, but rather
a useful computational trick for improving the accuracy of existing
significance testing techniques. Our code is available at
https://github.com/shuaideng1987/paired-permutation-test.
  Further, we propose a new statistical device -- hypervolume plot -- to
visualize the evidence against the null hypothesis, which can be used as a
auxiliary diagnostic tool for determining statistical significance.
Finally, we propose a new simple method for multiple-hypothesis testing based
on the hypervolume of the sampling space under the null hypothesis.
  Our study shows that the hypervolume of the sampling space can provide rich
information about the evidence against the null hypothesis, which can be used
to improve existing techniques for multiple-hypothesis testing.
  In particular, we show that the inverse of the expected hypervolume can be
used as a measure of the evidence against the null hypothesis, which can be
combined with p-values to improve the accuracy of conventional multiple-hypothesis
testing techniques.

for $L/D \gg 1$. Exploiting the index-matched nature of hydrogel grains in
water, we further show that the drag anisotropy is primarily caused by the
polystyrene grains themselves, and that the anisotropy would be negligible in
a bed of purely hydrogel grains, even at very large lengths scales.

for $|F_\perp-F_\parallel| \ll F_\perp+ F_\parallel$, which captures the
logarithmic dependence of the drag anisotropy on $L/D$.

Existing methods typically insert actors into the scene according to a set of
hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in their ability to model the true
complexity and diversity of real traffic scenes, thus inducing a content gap
between synthesized traffic scenes versus real ones. As a result, existing
simulators lack the fidelity necessary to train and test self-driving vehicles.
To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model
of traffic scenes that eschews the need for rules and heuristics. In
particular, given the ego-vehicle state and a high definition map of
surrounding area, SceneGen inserts actors of various classes into the scene and
synthesizes their sizes, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two
large-scale datasets SceneGen's ability to faithfully model distributions of
real traffic scenes. Moreover, we show that SceneGen coupled with sensor
simulation can be used to train perception models that generalize to the real
world.
  From a methodological perspective, SceneGen addresses two long-standing
challenges. First, the actor density and diversity produced by SceneGen are
guaranteed to satisfy the underlying distribution of real traffic scenes through
the use of a conditionally iterative decoder. Second, the HD map-based input
design combined with a factorized prediction model allows for a guarantee of
temporal and spatial plausibility of the generated scenes.
