9 local ultra/luminous infrared galaxies
(U/LIRGs) at $z <$ 0.04 through IFU observations with KOOLS-IFU on Seimei
Telescope. The observed targets are drawn from the Great Observatories All-sky
LIRG Survey (GOALS), covering a wide range of merger stages. We successfully
detect emission lines such as H$\beta$, [OIII]$\lambda$5007, H$\alpha$,
[NII]$\lambda\lambda$6549,6583, and [SII]$\lambda\lambda$6717,6731 with a
spectral resolution of $R$ = 1500-2000, which provides (i) spatially-resolved
($\sim$200-700 pc) moment map of ionized gas and (ii) diagnostics for active
galactic nucleus (AGN) within the central $\sim$3--11 kpc in diameter for our
sample. We find that [OIII] outflow that is expected to be driven by AGN tends
to be stronger (i) towards the galactic center and (ii) as a sequence of merger
stage. In particular, the outflow strength in the late-stage (stage D) mergers
is about 1.5 times stronger than that in the early-state (stage B) mergers,
which indicates that galaxy mergers could strengthen the AGN-driven outflow.
Notably, the outflow strength of [OIII] line is capable of depicting the
evolution of ionized outflow, and thus, the present result implies that the
stronger [OIII] outflow in late-stage mergers could be responsible, at least in
part, for the downscaling of star formation (SF) efficiency (i.e.,
$ \Sigma_{\rm SFR} / \Sigma_{\rm dust} $). Moreover, the present study suggests
that the role of ionized outflow in regulating SF in LIRGs is more pronounced
at larger spatial scales (from 0.6 to 7 kpc).
  Finally, the present trend of outflow-driven SF inhibition on larger scales
could be responsible for the diversity in the LIRG sample in terms of
presence/absence of AGN, and thus, our results may provide insight into the
link between galaxy mergers and AGN according to the scale under consideration.

the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the dominant coherent overturning
structures of convection.
  From this simple model we extract a coherent structure transport equation
analogous to that derived from direct numerical simulations of convection. This
simple model suggests that accurate prediction of the mean heat flux may be
possible from properties of individual coherent structures, potentially allowing
a much more efficient representation of convection in models.
  We discuss the potential of this simple analysis to inform improved closures
for multi-fluid convection models, and the further modelling work required. In
particular, the need to represent (without artificial restriction) the full
continuum of structure sizes is emphasised.
  Finally, we point out the broader potential of the multi-fluid paradigm to
re-examine and potentially greatly improve the treatment of sub-grid
variance closures in large-eddy simulation.

Twitter provides an opportunity to
assess public opinion on a topic directly from the people. However, Twitter
users often employ colloquialisms, abbreviations, and multiple words emoted as
a single word to convey their sentiments. Therefore, sentiment analysis on
Twitter is a challenging task. In this paper, we have trained a Part-of-speech
tagged (POS-tagged) dataset of around 20,000 tweets to perform the sentiment
task. We created the dataset by combining two existing datasets. We have
described the data collection process, data preprocessing steps, and the
results of cross-validation tests using Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier
as they demonstrate the effectiveness of the dataset for the sentiment analysis
task.
  We have also described a method to identify English, Hindi and Urdu tweets
from a multi-lingual dataset. We created a character level tagged dataset of
around 50,000 multi-lingual tweets by multi-tagging each tweet with its
respective languages. The dataset was created by lexically matching words in
multiple languages of each tweet with the vocabulary of the character-tagged
existing Hindi and Urdu dataset. We have described the data collection process,
data preprocessing steps and the results of cross-validation tests using SVM
classifier as they demonstrate the effectiveness of the dataset in identifying
the languages of the tweets.
  Both the datasets are available online for public use.

However, building a chat system is not scalable since it often requires a
considerable volume of data to work well, especially when enforcing
constraints such as being informative, engaging, or tailored to a
application. In this work, we explore the problem of conditional generation of
open-domain dialogues, where the model is trained on a few examples or
less. We propose Conditional Dialog Generation under Limited Data (CDLD), a
new task that addresses this problem. CDLD is challenging since there are two
aspects of constrained generation to capture: (1) task-level labels which are
expensive to obtain in large numbers and (2) the limited amount of training
data. To address CDLD, we first analyze the problem of limited data through a
theoretical lens and a set of empirical studies. The analyses lead to the
proposal of a range of methods that are inspired from priors and are
designed to work under the CDLD setting. We evaluate these methods on three
public dialog datasets and propose a suite of evaluation metrics that are
robust to the limited data situation. Our evaluation reveals that some of the
proposed methods work significantly better than a set of strong baselines and
validate the effectiveness of the proposed evaluation metrics. With CDLD, we
open a new methodology for evaluating and comparing models that can be a
starting point for further investigation.

chemotactic and antichemotactic behavior, depending on the strength of the
activity. Our coarse-grained Fokker-Planck approach yields an effective
potential, which we use to construct a nonequilibrium phase diagram that
classifies the dimers according to their tactic behavior. Moreover, we show

to the effect of a steering wheel in macroscopic devices. This work could be
useful for designing autonomous active colloidal structures which adjust their
motion depending on the local activity gradients.

this approach to a more challenging scenario in which even accessing the

on various benchmark networks and datasets. Experimental results demonstrate

dissimilarity matrix by adaptive singular value trimming and then compute the

propose a locally optimal transformation matrix to minimize the normal cross

efficient and effective knowledge distillation. Meanwhile, the factorized

NP-complete. We investigate and compare the computational complexity of both
decision problems restricted to some graph classes, deriving polynomial-time
algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and initial parameterized complexity
results, including an answer to an open question in the literature for the
complexity of SG for chordal graphs.

cardinality of the desired strong geodetic set, the Treewidth of~$G$, the

fixed-parameter tractable algorithms for problem (SG) with respect to each of
these parameters.

near-optimal expert demonstrations. However, high-quality demonstrations from
human experts can be expensive to obtain in large numbers. On the other hand,
it is often much easier to obtain large quantities of suboptimal or
task-agnostic trajectories, which are not useful for direct imitation, but can
nevertheless provide insight into the dynamical structure of the environment,
showing what could be done in the environment even if not what should be done.
We ask the question, is it possible to utilize such suboptimal offline datasets
to facilitate provably improved downstream imitation learning? In this work, we
answer this question affirmatively and present training objectives that use
offline datasets to learn a factored transition model whose structure enables
the extraction of a latent action space. Our theoretical analysis shows that
the learned latent action space can boost the sample-efficiency of downstream
imitation learning, effectively reducing the need for large near-optimal expert
datasets through the use of auxiliary non-expert data. To learn the latent
action space in practice, we propose TRAIL (Transition-Reparametrized Actions
for Imitation Learning), an algorithm that learns an energy-based transition
model contrastively, and uses the transition model to reparametrize the action
space for sample-efficient imitation learning. We evaluate the practicality of
our objective through experiments on a set of navigation and locomotion tasks.
Our results verify that a single noisy offline dataset can improve the sample
efficiency of downstream imitation learning by up to three orders of magnitude.

to improve the efficiency of
reinforcement learning by exploiting the expert demonstrations. However, in
many real scenarios, obtaining expert demonstrations could be extremely
expensive or even impossible. To overcome this challenge, in this paper, we
propose a novel learning framework called Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL) to
exploit the past good experiences of the agents themselves without expert
demonstration. Specifically, we train two different agents via letting each of
them alternately explore the environment and exploit the peer agent's
experience. While the experiences could be valuable or misleading, we propose
to estimate the potential utility of each piece of experience with the expected
gain of the value function. Thus the agents can selectively imitate from each
other by emphasizing the more useful experiences while filtering out noisy
ones. Experimental results on various tasks show significant superiority of the
proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework, validating that the agents can
benefit from each other without external supervision.
  Diving into the analysis of the proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework, we
observe a fascinating fact that, with certain exploration schemes, the agents
can even achieve better performance than using the expert demonstrations. This
wonderful property leads to another interesting question: "What are the
equivalent expert performances?" Answering this question, we further investigate
the lower bound of the cumulative reward that the agents can achieve through
co-imitation. To facilitate the analysis, we also provide a detailed proof of
the upper bound of the expected utility of each piece of experience. These two
bounds offer valuable insights into the trade-off between the estimation of the
expected utility and the exploration cost in the proposed framework.

(MLE) pre-training is a versatile method for enhancing neural machine
translation (NMT) performance. However, recent work has argued that the gains
produced by RL for NMT are mostly due to promoting tokens that have already
received a fairly high probability in pre-training. We hypothesize that the
large action space is a main obstacle to RL's effectiveness in MT, and conduct
two sets of experiments that lend support to our hypothesis. First, we find
that reducing the size of the vocabulary improves RL's effectiveness. Second,
we find that effectively reducing the dimension of the action space without
changing the vocabulary also yields notable improvement as evaluated by BLEU,
semantic similarity, and human evaluation. Indeed, by initializing the
network's final fully connected layer (that maps the network's internal
dimension to the vocabulary dimension), with a layer that generalizes over
similar actions, we obtain a substantial improvement in RL performance: 1.5
BLEU points on average.
  Our data comes from 1) multiple translation tasks, 2) multiple RL
objectives, 3) multiple evaluation metrics, and 4) multiple human evaluations.
We also show that by combining our method with RL applying MLE fine-tuning,
performance can be sustained at a higher level.
  Our method is simple to apply and requires no changes to the encoder network
and pre-training methodology. It is also computationally efficient as it only
needs to be applied to the decoder network.
  Overall, our study suggests that the challenge of applying RL to NMT is
fundamentally an high-dimensional one, and thus some form of dimension reduction
may be necessary to achieve meaningful improvement in MT performance with RL.
## Summary
Applied to the recent big-treasury multi-task setting, our method yields
notable improvement as evaluated by BLEU, semantic similarity, and human
evaluation.
  Our data comes from 1) multiple translation tasks, 2) multiple RL objectives,
3) multiple evaluation metrics, and 4) multiple human evaluations.
## Conclusion
Overall, our study suggests that the challenge of applying RL to NMT is
fundamentally an high-dimensional one, and thus some form of dimension reduction
may be necessary to achieve meaningful improvement in MT performance with RL.

role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users
alongside careful measurements of the time spent browsing various news sources.
We show that online news consumption follows a polarized pattern, where users'
visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show
that such preferences hold at the individual as well as the population level,
as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news domains
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of user choices in polarization. Are users simply following the links
proffered by their Web environment, or do they exacerbate partisan polarization
by intentionally pursuing like-minded news sources? To answer this question, we
compare browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure spanned by
the considered news domains, finding strong evidence of polarization in
partisan browsing habits beyond that which can be explained by the hyperlink
structure of the Web.
  In particular, our analysis reveals that the relative extent of polarization
in browsing habits versus hyperlink structure is so large that it cannot be
explained by a small set of powerful nodes, nor by a small set of influential
users. Rather, moderately influential users play a crucial role in
contributing to the Web's polarization, as excessive time spent on link
follow-up limits the ability of subsequent pages to attract attention.
Finally, we show that a novel model inspired by the rich get richer phenomenon
captures browsing patterns extremely well, with parameters sensitive to
changes in the hyperlink structure of the Web. This is the first time such a
model is successfully applied to study human behavior on the Web.
  In conclusion, we present a multifaceted analysis of the polarization of
Web browsing habits, with particular attention to the role of user choices.
Beyond describing the clear partisan communities of news domains that emerge,
our comparison of browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure
demonstrates that polarization is primarily due to differences in the way users
interact with the Web, rather than the structure of the Web itself.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.
  We offer a module (EG-CNN) that can be used to augment existing CNNs for
better boundary delineation and improve overall segmentation accuracy. We
publicly release our code at: https://github.com/AstraAI/EG-CNN.
  Segmentation tasks often rely on detecting edges before filling in the
segmentation mask. Therefore, techniques that efficiently capture edges are
vital for improvement in automated segmentation accuracy. Towards this, we
propose an efficient Edge-Gated Convolutional Neural Network (EG-CNN) that
inherently captures edges and is easily integratable with existing mainstream
segmentation architectures to further improve its performance. The EG-CNN is
designed with three novel ideas: a pre-trained domain invariant linear
transform to reduce dimensionality and increase independence of feature
representations, a parameter efficient gated convolution to emphasize edge
features, and a complementarity-based fusion to exploit the capability of the
gated convolution to produce enhanced feature representations near edges. We
assess the effectiveness of the EG-Cnn with various popular segmentation
algorithms on two publicly available datasets, KiTS 19 for kidney and BraTS 20
for brain tumor semantic segmentation. We demonstrate how the addition of
EG-Cnn consistently improves segmentation accuracy and generalization performance.

in the datasets, which causes lack of reliable unbias test datasets to valid

attribute, and then propose a novel bias identification framework for medical
image datasets. The framework contains two major components, KlotskiNet and
Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis(bdda), where KlostkiNet is to build the
mapping which makes backgrounds to distinguish positive and negative samples
and bdda provides a theoretical solution on determining bias attributes.

attributes discovered by the framework.

generalizability of the models trained on biased datasets through several
metrics. Results show that the generalizability of models is greatly improved

expanding universe is studied using
approximate analytic, and exact numerical solution of self-similar equations.
Both solutions have similar properties, which change qualitatively, depending
on the adiabatic powers $\gamma$. In the interval $1<\gamma<\gamma_{cr} \sim
1.16$ analytic and numeric solutions fill all the space without any voids and
they are rather close to each other. At larger $\gamma>\gamma_{cr}$ a pressure
becomes zero at finite radius, and a spherical void appears around the origin
in both solutions. All matter is collected in thin layer behind the shock wave
front. The structure of this layer qualitatively depends on $\gamma$. At the
inner edge of the layer the pressure is always zero, but the density on this
edge is jumping from zero to infinity at $\gamma \approx 1.4$ in both
solutions.
  Both solutions also have the common upper bound of $\gamma \approx 4$. At
larger $\gamma$ the solutions either become non-self-similar or invalid.
Counterexample is made to the statement that the self-similar solution of strong
shock wave propagating in the expanding universe corresponds to the adiabatic
index $\gamma=1$.
  It is shown that the main problem of the self-similar solutions, who do not
fill all the space, is not their non- validity, but their physical incorrectness
filling only outer parts of the system under consideration with the shock wave
front.
  Possible applications, and restrictions of the solutions are discussed.
In particular, it is shown that the analytic solution cannot give a correct
description of the matter distribution behind the shock wave front, if the
system under consideration has a finite size.
  Brief review of the similar problems is made.
  Conclusion is devoted to the possible generalization of the problem under
consideration to the continuous medium with the pressure.

chaotic behavior of the solutions is due to the collision of the interface

identified as the stick-slip region, where the clusters are not instantly

quasi-stationary with little cluster evolution.

performing the delta
hedging process of a European option. This cost is represented by an
integration formula that includes European option prices and a certain function
depending on the delta process. We first define a unit liquidity cost and then
show that the liquidity cost is a multiplication of the unit liquidity cost,
stock price, supply curve parameter, and the square of the number of options.
Using this formula, the expected liquidity cost before hedging can be
calculated much faster than when using a Monte Carlo simulation. Numerically
computed distributions of liquidity costs in special cases are also provided.
We show that on average, the liquidity cost of buying an option is opposite to
the liquidity cost of selling an option. Therefore, if market participants
have a preference for not engaging in a particular option buying/selling
transaction due to expected liquidity costs, they may want to consider
instead selling/buying the option, even if it means accepting a lower price.

Specifically, the malicious agents steer the network of agents away from the
optimal solution by sending false information to their neighbors and consume
significant bandwidth in the communication process. We propose a distributed
gradient-based optimization algorithm in which the non-malicious agents
exchange quantized information with one another. We prove convergence of the
solution to a neighborhood of the optimal solution, and characterize the
solutions obtained under the communication-constrained environment and presence

formulation. In Section III, we propose a distributed algorithm for optimization
with malicious agents. In Section IV, we analyze the stability and convergence
properties of the algorithm. Numerical simulations to illustrate the results are
presented in Section V. We conclude our work in Section VI.

  Word ordering is a constrained language generation task taking unordered

in the task. To explain why BART helps word ordering, we use probing on BART and
empirically identify that syntactic dependency knowledge in BART is a reliable

a random ensemble of
low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assume that the degree distributions of
the two ends of a randomly selected edge are independent. In the paper, we take
one step further and consider ensembles of LDPC codes with degree-degree
correlations. For this, we propose two methods to construct an ensemble of
degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. We then derive a system of density
evolution equations for such degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over a binary
erasure channel (BEC). By conducting extensive numerical experiments, we show
how the degree-degree correlation affects the performance of LDPC codes. Our
numerical results show that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation
could improve the maximum tolerable erasure probability. Moreover, increasing
the negative degree-degree correlation could lead to better unequal error
protection (UEP) design.
  Finally, we propose a method to construct degree-degree correlated LDPC codes
with superior decoding performance, by optimizing the degree-degree correlation
from a set of candidate ones. Our numerical results show that such a method
could be very efficient and produce good degree-degree correlated LDPC codes
without any explicit design effort.

Here we propose a hybrid measurement attack, with only linear optics, homodyne
detection, and single photon detection, to the widely used vacuum+weak decoy

We propose a hybrid measurement attack on the widely used hybrid QKD system with
vacuum+weak decoy state and partial phase randomization of source. That is, the
eavesdropper assumes the phase of source is partially, but not fully, randomized
as what he/ she should do to maximize the channel entropy if the phase is
completely random. Further, the hybrid attack incorporates not only homogeneous
homodyne detection but also inhomogeneous homodyne detection, which leads to a
better imitation of the signal states in the channel. Our simulation shows that
such a hybrid attack would result in an error rate very close to the optimal
error rate when the phase is completely random. That is, the eavesdropper is
able to steal all the key information without discovered by the users. Thus, our
proposal reveals that partial phase randomization is not sufficient to
guarantee the security of phase-encoding QKD systems with weak coherent states.
We also show how the hybrid attack performs when multi-photon events are
restricted. That is, our proposal reveals that the phase randomness of source is
not enough to guarantee the security of phase-encoding QKD systems, and the
restriction of the number of photons will limit the possible level of phase
randomization that can be achieved.

definition of the pressure and its unbiased estimators, several of which are
new. We further treat different sampling algorithms and crucial criteria for
bounding mixing times in the absence of analytical predictions. Our definite
results for the pressure, covering a wide range of densities, consistently
validate theoretical predictions based on mode-ranking techniques. We also
illustrate the superb sampling efficiency of event-chain algorithms when
combined with parallel tempering, leading to at least hundreds speedup
comparison to standard Monte Carlo. In addition, we suggest a number of
complex hard-disk systems that remain unsolved after the resolution of the
phase diagram.
  We show that the wide range of pressures values obtained in the past for the
hard-disk model all fall on a single universal curve, when properly scaled.
This universal curve, which is well-apparent from dimensional analysis, has
only recently been mathematically proven for the hard-disk model, and is
equivalent to the definition of the grand potential as a function of the
density and temperature. The universal pressure curve provides a crucial
benchmark for sampling algorithms. It also provides a protocol for obtaining
equilibrated states at high and low densities. We further illustrate several
examples of incorrectly computed pressures for systems in thermal
nonequilibrium.
  Finally, we propose a number of protocols for systematically checking for
equilibration in Monte Carlo simulations of continuous models.
  This work was done in part for the purpose of resolving several controversies
about the hard-disk model that have been raging for many decades. It is an
astonishing fact that so little attention has been given to the Computation
of pressures in these controversies. It is our hope that this detailed
treatment will be useful to future investigations of the hard-disk model,
which will likely be conducted from an perspective of comparing simulations to
necessary and sufficient theoretical criteria for the hard-disk phase
transition.

implemented as a smart contract and at its peak one of the largest consumers of

Forsage code both manually and using a purpose-built transaction simulator to

promotional videos and social media, we show how Forsage promoters have
leveraged the unique features of smart contracts to lure users with false
claims of trustworthiness and profitability, and how Forsage activity is
concentrated within a small number of national communities.

transparency of smart contract code and transactions to combat pyramid schemes
and protect users. It also suggests best practices for developers to avoid
accidentally building pyramid schemes when creating cryptocurrency contracts.

vulnerable and the importance of further research into the social and

-matter interaction in
first-principle tight-binding (TB) models. The standard way of describing
optical properties is the velocity gauge, defined by linear coupling to the
vector potential.
  In finite systems a transformation to represent the electromagnetic radiation
by the electric field instead is possible, albeit subtleties arise in periodic
systems. The resulting dipole gauge is a multi-orbital generalization of
Peierl's substitution. In this work, we investigate accuracy of both pathways,
with particular emphasis on gauge invariance, for TB models constructed from
maximally localized Wannier functions. Focusing on paradigmatic two-dimensional
materials, we construct first-principle models and calculate the response to
electromagnetic fields in linear response and for strong excitations.
Benchmarks against fully converged first-principle calculations allow for
ascertaining the accuracy of the TB models. We find that the dipole gauge
provides a more accurate description than the velocity gauge in all cases. The
main deficiency of the velocity gauge is an imperfect cancellation of
paramagnetic and diamagnetic current. Formulating a corresponding sum rule
however provides a way to explicitly enforce this cancellation. This procedure
corrects the TB models in the velocity gauge, yielding excellent agreement with
dipole gauge and thus gauge invariance.
  Our results provide a pathway for improving the description of light-matter
interaction in TB models. They are particularly relevant for studying optoelectrical
phenomena at ab-initio level, where often the focus is on understanding
specific properties which are sensitive to the electron-photon interaction.
Moreover, they open the pathway to investigate photoinduced phase transitions
and related dynamical critical behavior in TB models.
  Finally, we propose a simple way to gauge the accuracy of a TB model. We
assess this probe for various prototypes and for a monolayer layer transition
metallic rare earth compound. It provides valuable insights on the overall
accuracy of TB models and touches upon the issue of nodeless bands.

erasure correction code, we show that it cannot be both locally contractible
and sustain power-law correlation functions. Motivated by this no-go theorem,
and the desirability of local contractibility for an efficient variational
ansatz, we provide guidelines for constructing networks consisting of multiple
types of tensors that can support power-law correlation. We also provide an
explicit construction of one such network, which approximates the holographic
HaPPY pentagon code in the limit where variational parameters are taken to be
small.
  HaPPY has several desirable features, including being defined on a
two-dimensional lattice and having a small number of variational parameters.
However, its pentagon only approximates the bulk geometry of $\text{AdS}_3$,
which comes in different diameters. We discuss the limitations of this
approximation, and motivate a future study of network codes that are
'fully' approximating bulk $\text{AdS}_3$. Such an approximation could also be
useful for studying 2+1d quantum gravity phases, and could give us a
variational ansatz for studying certain classes of 2+1d quantum gravity models
that are currently not tractable.
  We also define and study a new network, the'star', which can be viewed as
a five-dimensional generalization of the HaPPY tetrahedron. The'star' can
fundamentally be used to build a large class of power-law networks, and has a
useful pattern of entanglement that can be used to build lines and planes.
Additionally, we show that the'star' can be used to approximate the
M2-brane bulk geometry of $\text{AdS}_4$, which could be useful for studying
quantum gravity in 3+1 dimensions.
  Finally, we show that both the HaPPY network and the'star' can be
interpreted as codes that repair quantum errors corrupting large regions of
space. This is by viewing them as codes that approximately implement
'erasure correction' over large distances.

retinal chromophore in rhodopsin was
computationally studied using a two-state two-mode model coupled to thermal
baths. Reaction quantum yields at the steady state (10 ps and beyond) were
found to be considerably different than their transient values, suggesting a
weak correlation between transient and steady-state dynamics in these systems.
Significantly, the steady-state quantum yield was highly sensitive to minute
changes in system parameters, while transient dynamics was nearly unaffected.
Correlation of such sensitivity with standard level spacing statistics of the
nonadiabatic vibronic system suggests a possible origin in quantum chaos. The
feasibility of experimental observation of this phenomenon and its implications
in condensed-phase photochemistry and biological light sensing are discussed.
Overall, our results indicate that transient and steady-state photochemistry
may be governed by different physical phenomena.

Neural Networks (CNN) and Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been successfully used for process-mining tasks.
They have achieved better performance for different predictive tasks than
traditional approaches. We extend the existing body of research by testing four
different variants of Graph Neural Networks (GNN) and a fully connected
Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) with dropout for the tasks of predicting the
nature and timestamp of the next process activity. In contrast to existing
studies, we evaluate our models' performance at different stages of a process,
determined by quartiles of the number of events and normalized quarters of the
case duration. This provides new insights into the performance of a prediction
model, as they behave differently at different stages of a business-process.
Interestingly, our experiments show that the simple MLP often outperforms more
sophisticated deep-learning models in both prediction tasks. We argue that care
needs to be taken when applying automated process-prediction techniques at
different stages of a process. We further argue that researchers should reflect
their results with strong baselines methods like simple MLPs.
  From an application perspective, our findings suggest that practitioners
should consider using simpler models like MLPs for process-prediction tasks.
These models are often simpler to train and deploy compared to deep-learning
models. Further research is needed to build more effective but easier to fit
process prediction models.

  We present a method for multi-task generalization that learns a set of
related dynamical systems with a low-dimensional set of latent factors. This
method, called Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), is
useful for learning and generalizing from multiple related situations with
reoccurring contexts and tasks. HiP-RSSMs avoids the need for extra inputs
encoding the latent factors and relatedness by parameterizing the dynamics
with: (1) a task-independent part that generalizes across tasks and (2) a
low-dimensional latent factor part that generalizes across contexts within a
task. We present an efficient method for learning and performing inference over
the Gaussian graphical model, by combining algebraic simplifications with the
power of modern computational libraries. HiP-RSSMs outperforms single task
state-space models and related multi-task methods on several benchmarks for
both simulation and real world experimentation.

for understanding and
studying political polarization in political and social systems. Several
methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some
of the methods are sensitive to degree distributions and relative sizes of the
polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization, after which most of the methods have better performance than the
best-performing method before normalization. This work opens up the possibility
to critically assess and compare the features and performance of different
methods for measuring structural polarization.
  From a mathematical perspective, the problem of measuring structural
polarization boils down to regressing the amount of polarization (a physical
quantity) from some structural features (measurements of structure) and it is
important to take the full range of possible values of the feature into
consideration. In statistics, the concept of variance is used to capture the
full range of possible values of a quantity and its degradation in quality
demonates a lack of understanding of the phenomenon being studied. Variance of
degree distribution has been used by some researchers as a measure of
polarization and we show that it fails to capture the amount of polarization in
a simple toy model.
  From a physical perspective, the concept of variance inherently implies the
existence of a mean which is typically lost in network research. The mean of
degree distribution in several networks is less than 1 indicating that these
networks are not adequate to study polarization among two distinct groups of
nodes.
  Further, all physical systems show a variation in their properties around
their mean properties. Therefore, it is crucial to have a proper understanding
of the mean and variation of degree distribution in the context of
polarization. Research on polarization has been done using several measures of
variation like variance, coefficient of variation but none of these measures
have been applied on the variation of the fraction of poles (not degree) in a
network.

generate hyper-prompts: we propose HyperPrompt, a novel architecture for
prompt-based task-conditioning of self-attention in Transformers. HyperPrompt
is a hyper network that takes task-specific hyper-prompts as input and outputs
hyper-weights. These hyper-weights are used to multiply the pre-trained
task-conditioning prompts to generate hyper-prompts, which are used to attend
to task-conditioned features. We show that hyper-prompts learned with
HyperPrompt achieve significant gains over both static prompts and auxiliary
learning of task representations without using additional parameters. We
perform extensive experiments on both classification and sentence-level
prediction tasks across 8 datasets spanning 8 languages, as well as the
CommonSenseReasoning dataset. Results show that HyperPrompt achieves up to
$7.0$ accuracy points improvement and $2.0$ F1-point improvement over the
baseline.
  We also explore that HyperPrompt is a generalization of QuickDial and
AutoPrompt. Results show that HyperPrompt achieves substantial gains over
QuickDial and AutoPrompt across 8 languages and 10 tasks, often outperforming
these parameter-efficient methods by a large margin.

  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\},

is bounded, then a Sobolev regularity assumption on the gradient of the
obstacle $\psi$ transfers to the gradient of the solution, provided the partial
map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a Sobolev space, $W^{1, p+2}$. The
novelty here is that we deal with subquadratic growth conditions with respect
to the gradient variable, i.e. $f(x, \xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ with $1<p<2,$ and
where the map $a$ belongs to a Sobolev space.
  We complement a result of Gilardi in which a stronger assumption, namely
log-H\"older continuity of the function $a,$ was required in order to get
differentiability of the solution with respect to the gradient of the obstacle.
In particular our result completes the study of the dependence on the regularity
of the obstacle started in our previous work.
  Finally we show a result in which the regularity of the obstacle is translated
into the same class of the gradient of the solution; in particular if $\psi\in
C^{1,\alpha},$ for $\alpha>1-p,$ then $Du\in C^{1,\alpha}.$
  Our approach is based on a new strategy developed by the authors in order to
transfer gradient regularity of the obstacle to the solution; in particular we
prove a new non-decay estimate.

ofiller-modified polymer matrices have
immense potential to improve the safety of high-risk engineering structures.
These materials are intrinsically self-sensing because their electrical
conductivity is affected by deformations and damage. This property, known as
piezoresistivity, has been extensively leveraged for conductivity-based damage
detection via electrical resistance change methods and tomographic imaging
techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Although these
techniques are very effective at detecting the presence of damage, they suffer
from an inability to provide precise information about damage shape, size, or
mechanism. This is particularly detrimental for laminated composites which can
suffer from complex failure modes, such as delaminations, that are difficult to
detect. To that end, we herein propose a new technique for precisely
determining damage shape and size in self-sensing composites. Our technique
makes use of a genetic algorithm (GA) integrated with realistic physics-based
damage models to recover precise damage shape from conductivity changes imaged
via EIT. We experimentally validate this technique on carbon nanofiber
(CNF)-modified glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates by considering
two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. Our results
show that this novel technique can accurately reconstruct multiple
through-holes with radii as small as 1.5 mm and pressures to predict delamination
shape and size. We further show that this technique can be improved by
fine-tuning the damage model to better fit the underlying physics of
conductivity change due to damage. Furthermore, we find that the conductivity
change due to through-holes is accurately predicted by a GA-optimized
theoretical model, while the conductivity change due to delaminations is better
predicted by a GA-optimized machine learning model. Overall, this work presents
a novel approach towards quantitatively assessing damage in self-sensing
composites using EIT and GA-based algorithms.

students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different demographic groups. Student learning data is collected from 70 online
learning modules assigned as both online homework and self-study material in
both Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules being
assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Students' ability to stay on
track is measured by three data indicators: percentage of modules submitted
before the due date, percentage of modules submitted early for extra credit,
and percentage of modules properly engaged with. The student population is
divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Exam and course scores are also compared
between demographics groups in Fall 2020 and against scores from the Fall 2019
semester. The analysis revealed that remote learning significantly reduced
on-time and early submission for first-generation students, but increased the
frequency of early submission for transfer students. Under-represented minority
students had higher percentage of engaged modules during the pandemic, while
non-URM students had lower. Women had higher percentage of engaged modules than
men during the pandemic. First-generation students and non-URM students had
lowerer exam scores in Fall 2020 compared to Fall 2019.

define well-studied, continuous distributions over network instances, and are
increasingly used for inferring evolutionary histories from gene sequences.
Stochastic phylogenetic networks also provide framework for Bayesian inference

assures that in practice they produce categorical margins. Knowing the
exactly marginal densities is crucial for quantifying the uncertainty in the
inferred network and its edge weights, and thus in Bayesian inference. However,
computation of these margins is intractable. In this work we present an upper
bound on the marginal density of an edge weight in the context of the Dirichlet
process. We show through simulation that this bound is tight; and we hope that
this tightness will be used towards developing sampling methods for the exact
margins.

stochastic phylogenetic networks, called the reticulate index. Reticulate
information encoded in a network is captured by the difference between the
number
of reticulate and linear trajectories from its root to its leaves. Analysis of
this quantity in simulation and on real data leads interesting insights on the

biases in estimation of phylogenetic networks. We define a modification of

currently provide the most feasible roadmap towards large-scale fault-tolerant
quantum computation. As such, obtaining fast and flexible decoding algorithms
for these codes, within the experimentally relevant context of faulty syndrome
measurements, is of critical importance. In this work, we show that the problem
of decoding such codes, in the full fault-tolerant setting, can be naturally
reformulated as a process of repeated interactions between a decoding agent and
a code environment, to which the machinery of reinforcement learning can be
applied to obtain decoding agents. As a demonstration, by using deepQ learning,
we obtain fast decoding agents for the surface code, for a variety of
noise-models.
  We find that for the noise models considered, an amazingly small number of
learning steps is required to obtain optimal performance. Furthermore, the
learning process is universal, in the sense that a learning trajectory is
capable of producing decent performance for noise parameters it has never
encountered before. We also show that there exists a narrow gap between the
performance of the best possible decoding agents (up to our noise model
assumptions) and what the learning process is capable of producing.
  Finally, we show that a surprisingly small decoding agent is capable of
reproducing the full trajectory of a learned decoding function. This may open
paths towards running learned surface code decoders on hardware.
  Last but not least, we work out detailed learning trajectories for two natural
bottlenecks in decoding - the case of faulty syndrome readout, and the case of
long error chains.
  All of the presented learning trajectories result from straightforward
learning, and as such we believe that there is potential for further performance
boost through the use of more advanced reinforcement learning techniques.
Last but not least, all of the presented decoding agents can be directly
projected onto a set of simple perceptrons, which is demonstrated in the main
text, and may open the possibility of running learned decoders on hardware.

network architecture and performance may differ significantly. For example,
these systems use fundamentally different network transport and routing
protocols, which may introduce network noise that can eventually limit the

bandwidth, and collective communication patterns in detailed small-scale
measurements, and then we simulate network performance at a larger scale. We
validate our approach on four popular cloud providers and three on-premise HPC
systems, showing that network (and also OS) noise can significantly impact
performance and cost both at small and large scale.

significant differences exist between them and on-premise systems. Further, we

same scope may fail due to network limitations in both cloud and on-premise

may impact overall cost by up to 40%. In summary, our detailed simulations and
small-scale measurements aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of
cloud-on-premise comparisons from the network perspective, which is important
for developing optimal strategies for cloud adoption and for developing
stronger, more reliable software.

observed process behavior recorded in event data. Alignments are a
state-of-the-art technique to detect, localize, and quantify deviations in
process executions, i.e., traces, compared to reference process models.
Alignments, however, assume complete process executions covering the entire
process from start to finish or prefixes of process executions. This paper
defines infix/postfix alignments, proposes approaches to their computation, and
evaluates them using real-life event data.
  We define infix/postfix alignments and propose approaches to their computation.
Our approaches are based on regular expressions and are defined recursively
following the structure of process models. We evaluate them using event data
collected from the air traffic control process, banking process, and two
processes from the medical domain. The case studies show that regular expressions
can be used to define alignments in a automated manner and provide insights
into the performance of regular expressions.
  While regular expressions provide a practical way of defining infix and
postfix alignments, they rely on heuristics and are not guaranteed to compute
all possible alignments. Therefore, we propose a technique to define regular
expressions that are more expressive than their heuristic counterparts. The
technique is based on automata and guarantees completeness of alignments.
Although the approach is more complex than regular expressions, it is efficient
and can handle large process models.
  In addition to regular expressions, we define an extension that enables the
specification of frequency alignments. Extensions of regular expressions with
frequency alignments are capable of defining all simple linear temporal
logic formulas.
  Infix and postfix alignments are important for process understanding, process
improvement, and process discovery. Process improvements, for example, can use
postfix alignments to improve process transitions that are equipped with
process costs (i.e., prices) and infix alignments to improve process paths
equipped with process costs. Process discovery can benefit from infix and
postfix alignments to evaluate and structure the discovered process models.
Further research is needed to understand the applications of infix and postfix
alignments and their impact on process understanding, process improvement, and
process discovery.

assumed that the complexity of measuring this new system call graph is
polynomially related to the number of the nodes of the call graph. Thus, our
approach is to apply singular value decomposition on the matrix of the system
call graph, then on the reduced matrix to determine the parts that affect the
performance of the system and to identify these parts for re-examination. The
time complexity of our algorithm is polynomially related to the number of the
nodes of the call graph. Using the experimental system, our algorithm, and the
hardware (shared memory systems) produced very good results in terms of
accuracy and speedup.

long history in mathematics, going back to Bachet and Lagrange. While for some
specific rings (like integers or polynomials over the rationals), there are
known methods for decomposing an element into a sum of squares, in general, for
many other important rings and fields, the problem is still widely open. In
this paper, we present an explicit algorithm for decomposing an element of an
arbitrary global field (either a number field or a global function field) into
a sum of squares of minimal length.
  From a number theoretic perspective, this work amounts to an explicit
algorithms for computing a Hermite normal form of the ideal generated by the
input element, using a combination of standard ideal theory techniques
(especially arithmetic of ring of integers, ideal classification, and computation
of ray class fields) and recent results on the computability of maximal
orders in the rational adele group, which provide the necessary control on the
size of the result. The present work does not make use of any of the existing
algorithms for totally positive decomposition, which go all the way back to the
works of Bachet and Lagrange. In particular, our algorithm does not require any
quadratic forms machinery, which is the main ingredient in all previous
algorithms.
  We experimentally evaluate our algorithm on two kinds of inputs: (1) randomly
sampled elements of these fields and (2) homogeneous polynomials. The results
show that in the case of global function fields the algorithm is very fast
(compared to the size of the input) while in the case of global number fields
it is a bit slower.
  We also show that in the case of quadratic fields our algorithm is
equivalent to the classical Lagrange's algorithm for totally positive
decomposition. Furthermore, for the field Q(x) of rational functions over the
rational numbers we consider the notion of totally positive decomposition with
respects to a given norm. We present an algorithm for computing such a
decomposition when the norm is induced by a place of degree one.
  Finally, we work out a few interesting examples of totally positive
decompositions in algebraic number fields and global fields of characteristic
$p>0$.

spectroscopy where the spectral cross-correlation with a template spectrum can

designed, modulated transmission spectrum, the cross-correlation can be carried
out optically without requiring any dispersion, vastly simplifying the
instrument and reducing its cost. The measured correlation lag can be used for
detecting atomic/molecular species within and determining the radial velocity
of a particular astrophysical object.

developed that use different photonic platforms: silicon and fibre-based
photonics. The silicon photonic approach utilizes ring resonators that can be
thermo-optically modulated to carry out the cross-correlation. The fibre
approach uses customized fibre Bragg gratings (FBGs) with transmission spectra
that can be strain-modulated. Both approaches have been able to detect
molecular gas in a lab setting, and we are now in the process of on-sky
testing.

  Relational machine learning models for drug data attempt to capture
associations between drugs. These associations can be represented as graphs,
matrix tables and other data structures. Here, we provide a comparison of
single-layer and multi-layer data representation in the context of drug data.
We argue that single-layer representations are sufficient for many tasks, but
multi-layer representations can capture higher-order relationships between
drugs. Finally, we discuss how choice of representation can have an impact on
model performance and generalization.
  Beyond data representation, model choice is a crucial aspect of drug machine
learning. Here, we provide a comparison of the most common model classes,
including logistic regression, neural networks and graph neural networks, in
the context of drug data. We argue that graph neural networks are particularly
suitable for drug data, as they can learn task-specific graph layers which can
capture associations between drugs. Finally, we discuss how model choice can
have an impact on performance and generalization.
  Performance of drug machine learning models depends on various factors. In
this section, we provide a comparison of performance metrics, an evaluation of
existing datasets and a discussion of important issues such as overfitting and
the influence of noise in the data.

possible future extensions of the proposed models. Finally, we provide a list of
important references to related work on graph neural networks and relational

learning once the number of active clients increases. The \textit{FedBuff}
algorithm (Nguyen et al., 2022) alleviates this problem by allowing
asynchronous updates (staleness), which enhances the scalability of training
while preserving privacy via secure aggregation. We revisit the
\textit{FedBuff} algorithm for asynchronous federated learning and extend the
existing analysis by removing the boundedness assumptions from the gradient
norm. This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the convergence rate of
this algorithm when heterogeneity in data, batch size, and delay are
considered.
  Let $R$ be the maximum delay, $K$ be the number of active clients, and
$n_k$ be the local sample size of the $k$th client. We show that the convergence
rate is $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{R}{\min_{k} n_k} + \frac{R}{K} \right)$ when the
gradient is unbounded and the step size satisfies $0 < \eta \leq \frac{1}{L}$, where
$L$ is the learning rate of the client's local update, is known. In addition, we
present a proof of the convergence of the optimization error when the step size
satisfies $0 < \eta \leq \frac{1}{\mu}$, where $\mu$ is the eigenvalue of the
federated matrix inversion, in a familiar symmetric environment where
$n_k=n$ for all $k$.
  We conduct experiments on three typical datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and
Sports (human action recognition). The results show that the proposed algorithm
achieves a good balance between the improvement in accuracy and an increase in
the number of active clients as well as allowed delay.

state-of-the-art results, but they require large datasets and extensive
computing resources. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome these
difficulties even across languages, e.g., German ASR trained from an English
model. We experiment with much less related languages, reusing an English model
for Czech ASR. To simplify the transfer, we propose to use an intermediate
alphabet, Czech without accents, and document that it is a highly effective
strategy. The technique is also useful on Czech data alone, in the style of
coarse-to-fine training. We achieve substantial eductions in training time as
well as word error rate (WER).
  We also observe a strong effect of the model size adaptation to the Czech
dataset. Thus we propose to adapt the dimensionality of the embedding and
RNN layers from the original English model to the Czech dataset. Our method has
the advantage of not requiring pre-trained tall model components, as was done
before. We document several reusable parameterization settings for both the
models and the data.
  The best single result achieved (WER=26.5%) is only 2% worse than the
best-end-to-end Czech result we could find in the literature, which was obtained
with a large amount of finely-tuned neural network layers, while we use only
two-level end-to-end system. Therefore we conclude that our system is a
competitive, transfer learning-based end-to-end Czech ASR system.
  Finally, we release our Czech corpus, the Prague University of Technology
(PVT) corpus, which was prepared in the spirit of shared resources for
developing ASR and NLP systems for Czech.

around the invariant mass $1.5~\rm GeV$ of a $K_SK_S$ pair, which
$\rho^0(1450)$ cannot decay into because of Bose-Einstein statistics, can be
accounted for by a nonresonant $S$-wave $K_SK_S$ component. We therefore
conclude that the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance can explain the state

in more $B$-meson decays.

the rate of Hawking radiation slows down for black holes perceiving the dark

for a species scale of ${\cal O}(10^{10}~{\rm GeV})$, an all-dark-matter

region. We also show that PBHs with $M_{\rm BH} \sim 10^{12}~{\rm g}$ could
potentially explain the well-known Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line if they make
up a tiny fraction of the total dark matter density.
  Finally, we compute the thermal retention factor of a black hole surrounded by
a heat bath spanning the extra-dimensional realm. We demonstrate that, for some
range of temperatures, below the Bohr temperature but still quite high, the
thermal retention factor is enhanced compared to the 4D case up to a couple of
orders of magnitude for small extra-dimensional scales.

(TD) learning that addresses
several challenges faced by robots learning to navigate in a marine
environment. For improved data efficiency, our method reduces TD updates to
Gaussian Process regression. To make predictions amenable to online settings,
we introduce a sparse approximation with improved quality over current
rejection-based sparse methods. We derive the predictive value function
posterior and use the moments to obtain a new algorithm for model-free policy
evaluation, SPGP-SARSA. With simple changes, we show SPGP-SARSA can be reduced
to a model-based equivalent, SPGP-TD. We perform comprehensive simulation
studies and also conduct physical learning trials with an underwater robot. Our
results show SPGP-SARSA can outperform the state-of-the-art sparse method,
replicate the prediction quality of its exact counterpart, and be applied to
solve underwater navigation tasks.
  We make the following open-source contributions from our work: (1) a new
python package `gpylearn` for Gaussian Process modeling in the context of
robotics/ML, (2) a python implementation of SPGP-SARSA for model-free policy
evaluation and SPGP-TD for model-based policy evaluation available as a
contributor to the popular underwater robot simulator package `guppy`, and (3)
a python/script framework for simulating generic continuous control tasks with
easy-to-use defaults.

comparators of arity $k > 2$. That is, in our setting the arity of the
comparators -- or, in other words, the number of inputs that can be sorted at
the unit cost -- is a parameter. We study its relationship with two other
parameters -- $n$, the number of inputs, and $d$, the depth.
  This model received considerable attention. Partly, its motivation is to
better understand the structure of sorting networks. In particular, sorting
networks with large arity are related to recursive constructions of ordinary
sorting networks. Additionally, studies of this model have natural
correspondence with a recent line of work on constructing circuits for majority
functions from majority gates of lower fan-in.
  Motivated by these questions, we obtain the first lower bounds on the arity
of constant-depth sorting networks. More precisely, we consider sorting
networks of depth $d$ up to 4, and determine the minimal $k$ for which there is
such a network with comparators of arity $k$. For depths $d=1,2$ we observe
that $k=n$. For $d=3$ we show that $k = \lceil \frac n2 \rceil$. For $d=4$ the
minimal arity becomes sublinear: $k = \Theta(n^{2/3})$. This contrasts with the
trivially achievable (and necessary) bound of $k \geq \lceil \frac n2 \rceil$.
  To establish these bounds, we also show that if $A(d,n,k)$ denotes the number
of wires in the best (minimal) depth-$d$ sorting network using comparators of
arity $k$, then $A(4,n,2n^{1/3}) = \Theta(n^{2/3} \cdot 2^n)$. This might be
viewed as a deepness version of Babai and Szemer\'edi's $A(o(1),n,k)=\Theta(k\cdot
2^n)$.
  Finally, we construct a depth-4 sorting network using comparators of arity 3
and approximately $2^{7/3}$ wires. This gives another lower bound on the
arity, which is close to the square root of $n$ for large $n$.

mergers are able to have a transformative effect on galaxy morphology. In this
paper, we investigate the role of magnetic fields in gas-rich major mergers. To
this end, we run a series of high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) zoom-in
simulations with the moving-mesh code Arepo and compare the outcome with
hydrodynamic simulations run from the same initial conditions. This is the
first time that the effect of magnetic fields in major mergers has been
investigated in a cosmologically-consistent manner. In contrast to previous
non-cosmological simulations, we find that the inclusion of magnetic fields has
a substantial impact on the production of the merger remnant. Whilst magnetic
fields do not strongly affect global properties, such as the star formation
history, they are able to significantly influence structural properties.
Indeed, MHD simulations consistently form remnants with extended discs and
well-developed spiral structure, whilst hydrodynamic simulations form more
compact remnants that display distinctive ring morphology. We support this work
with a resolution study and show that whilst global properties are broadly
converged across resolution and physics models, morphological differences only
develop given sufficient resolution. We argue that this is due to the more
efficient excitement of a small-scale dynamo in higher resolution simulations,
resulting in a more strongly amplified field that is better able to influence
gas dynamics. We argue that the predicted presence of spiral structure in
observed merger remnants is able to constrain the role of magnetic fields in
these systems. Furthermore, the predicted presence of spiral structure in
modelled galaxy discs is able to constrain the richness of the simulated
magnetic fields.
  We find that magnetic fields are able to create a more dynamic and
asymmetric merger geometry, with a larger central peak in the gas density and
a longer tail. This is able to influence the production of the merger remnant,
with the inclusion of magnetic fields effectively preventing the merger of the
two central peaks into a single ring feature. Furthermore, we find that
magnetic fields are able to regulate the formation of a disc in the merger
remnant, with MHD simulations consistently displaying more extended discs than
hydrodynamic simulations. Indeed, the disc in an MHD merger remnant is able to
capture features similar to those observed in the Milky Way, such as a central
bar and a large central bulge.

experiments and model calculations. The two inequivalent Gd$^{3+}$ ions form
the centered honeycomb lattice, which consists of honeycomb and triangular
sublattices. The dc magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements
suggest two antiferromagnetic phase transitions at $T_\textrm{N1}$ = 2.3 K and
$T_\textrm{N2}$ = 1.02 K. An inflection point is observed in the isothermal
magnetization curve, which implies an up-up-down phase with a 1/3 magnetization
plateau. We also observe a large magnetic entropy change originated from the
magnetic frustration in GdInO$_3$. By considering a classical spin Hamiltonian,
we establish the ground state phase diagram, which suggests that GdInO$_3$ has
a weak easy-axis anisotropy and is close to the equilateral triangular-lattice
system. The theoretical ground-state phase diagram may be used as a reference
in NMR, ESR, or $\mu$SR experiments in future.
  In conclusion, GdInO$_3$ exhibits complex magnetic properties and has a
1/3 magnetization plateau, which makes it an interesting candidate for both
fundamental research of quantum magnetism and application in magnetic memory
devices. Our results also suggest that rare-earth indium oxides may favor
triplanes antiferromagnetic order, which is currently rarely observed in
solids. Further investigation of these intriguing ground states is highly
desirable.

allocations in the non-strategic setting: Round-Robin (EF1 allocations for any

that are EF1 with respect to the underlying true values, while for the
algorithm of Plaut and Roughgarden we show that the corresponding allocations
not only are EFX but also satisfy maximin share fairness, something that is
impossible for homogeneous agents.

is data-centric, of
which one fundamental challenge is to understand the influence of data quality
to ML training -- "Which training examples are 'guilty' in making the trained
ML model predictions inaccurate or unfair?" Modeling data influence for ML
training has attracted intensive interest over the last decade, and one popular
framework is to compute the Shapley value of each training example with respect
to utilities such as validation accuracy and fairness of the trained ML model.
Unfortunately, despite recent intensive interest and research, existing methods
only consider a single ML model "in isolation" and do not consider an
end-to-end ML pipeline that consists of data transformations, feature
extractors, and ML training.
  We present DataScope (ease.ml/datascope), the first system that efficiently
computes Shapley values of training examples over an end-to-end ML pipeline,
and illustrate its applications in data debugging for ML training. To this end,
we first develop a novel algorithmic framework that computes Shapley value over
a specific family of ML pipelines that we call canonical pipelines: a positive
relational algebra query followed by a K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) classifier. We
show that, for many subfamilies of canonical pipelines, computing Shapley value
is in PTIME, contrasting the exponential complexity of computing Shapley value
in general. We then put this to practice -- given an sklearn pipeline as input,
automate the process of computing Shapley value over the underlying relational
data. We further introduce a novel optimization that makes the computation
efficient -- instead of repurposing the relational data used to train the KNN
classifier for computing Shapley value, we create a specialized data structure
called a Ball Index, which significantly reduces the relational data access
costs.
  We experiment with several ML pipelines learned over three diverse datasets
(LFW, MNIST, and IMDB). DataScope reduces the cost of computing Shapley value by
an order of magnitude compared to a generic computer programming framework like
SymPy. Further, DataScope returns interesting insights on data quality, which
could be used to improve the dataset.
  We hope that DataScope paves the way towards developing a suite of tools that
can debug ML training data.

millisecond pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries (XRBs), the dependence of

hypergraphs; however, their datasets often end up being published or studied

issue, we first establish a theoretical framework to characterize this issue's
implications and worst-case scenarios. The analysis motivates our formulation
of the new task, supervised hypergraph reconstruction: reconstructing a
real-world hypergraph from its projected graph, with the help of some existing
knowledge of the application domain.

in the projection, based on which we create a framework containing two modules:
(1) to handle the enormous search space of potential hyperedges, we design a
sampling strategy with efficacy guarantees that significantly narrows the space
to a smaller set of candidates; (2) to identify hyperedges from the candidates,
we further design a hyperedge classifier in two well-working variants that
capture structural features in the projection. Extensive experiments validate
our claims, approach, and extensions. Remarkably, our approach outperforms all
baselines by an order of magnitude in accuracy on hard datasets. Our code and
data can be downloaded from bit.ly/SHyRe.

learning on hypergraphs. This work opens the door to new deep learning ideas
and applications on hypergraphs. We hope this success will encourage more
research into supervised hypergraph reconstruction and other analyses of
hypergraph data.

in hypergraph projections. This framework can lead to a new suite of benchmark
datasets, which we initiate with three large social network benchmarks. The
benchmark creation ideally requires a survey of existing social network
studies. We attempt this with a new systematic analysis of social network
datasets. In this analysis, we further derive the first social network
generator based on empirical observations, which when used in a hypergraph
setting, leads to several interesting results on the structure of hypergraphs.

expertise on social structures.
  Overall, this research marks significant progress in the analysis of complex
systems by developing a framework to evaluate hypergraph data retrieved as
graphs, and by initiating a new avenue of research with the systematic analysis
of social network datasets.

) aims to learn effective
multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, which is an important step
toward the deployment of multi-agent systems in real-world applications.
However, in practice, each individual behavior policy that generates
multi-agent joint trajectories usually has a different level of how well it
performs. e.g., an agent is a random policy while other agents are medium
policies. In the cooperative game with global reward, one agent learned by
existing offline MARL often inherits this random policy, jeopardizing the
performance of the entire team. In this paper, we investigate offline MARL with
explicit consideration on the diversity of agent-wise trajectories and propose
a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to address this
problem. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network assigns
the credit to each agent through a differentiable key-value memory mechanism in
an offline manner. These decomposed credits are then used to reconstruct the
joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay with individual
trajectories, thereafter agents can share their good trajectories and
conservatively train their policies with a graph attention network (GAT) based
critic. We evaluate our method in both discrete control (i.e., StarCraft II and
multi-agent particle environment) and continuous control (i.e, multi-agent
mujoco). The results indicate that our method achieves significantly better
results in complex and mixed offline MARL scenarios.

clusters (NSCs) with a semi-analytical approach for early structure formation.
Within this framework, we keep track of the dynamics of Pop III binary (compact
object) remnants during cosmic structure formation, and construct the
population of Pop III binary remnants that fall into NSCs by dynamical friction
of field stars. The subsequent evolution within NSCs is then derived from
three-body encounters and gravitational-wave (GW) emission. We find that 7.5%
of Pop III binary remnants will fall into the centres ($< 3\ \rm pc$) of
galaxies. About $5-50\%$ of these binaries will merge at $z>0$ in NSCs,
including those with very large initial separations (up to 1~pc). The merger
rate density (MRD) peaks at $z\sim 5-7$ with $\sim 0.4-10\ \rm yr^{-1}\ \rm
Gpc^{-3}$, leading to a promising detection rate $\sim 170-2700\ \rm yr^{-1}$
for 3rd-generation GW detectors that can reach $z\sim 10$. Low-mass ($\lesssim
10^{6}\ \rm M_{\odot}$) NSCs formed at high redshifts ($z\gtrsim 4$) will
preserve more Pop III binaries, and these will merge at a higher rate
($\gtrsim 1\ \rm yr^{-1}\ \rm Gpc^{-3}$) at $z\leq 0$. We also find that GW
emission is not effective in unbinding Pop III binaries, and the effect of
three-body encounters depends on the initial mass function of NSCs. Our results
suggest that future GW detectors will provide a promising pathway to probe
the formation and evolution of NSCs, and, in turn, the Pop III binary remnant
fruition.
  Finally, we discuss the implications of our results from different formation
models of NSCs, and the potential to probe Pop III binaries with 21~cm
recombination line observations.

of human beings. Scientific
literature, as the major medium that carries knowledge between scientists,
exhibits explosive growth during the last century. Despite the frequent use of
many tangible measures, such as citation, impact factor and g-index, to
quantify the influence of papers from different perspectives based on
scientific productivity, it has not yet been well understood how the
relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge amount turns out to
be, i.e., how the knowledge value of papers and knowledge amount vary with
development of the discipline. This raises the question of whether high
scientific productivity equals large knowledge amount. Here, building on rich
literature on academic conferences and journals, we collect 185 million
articles covering 19 disciplines published during 1970 to 2020, and establish
citation network research area to represent the knowledge flow from the authors
of the article being cited to the authors of the articles that cite it under
each specific area. As a result, the structure formed during the evolution of
each scientific area can implicitly tells how the knowledge flows between nodes
and how it behaves as the number of literature (productivity) increases. By
leveraging Structural entropy in structured high-dimensional space and Shannon
entropy in unstructured probability space, we propose the Quantitative Index of
Knowledge (KQI), which is taken as the subtraction between the two types of
entropy, to reflect the extent of disorder of the system, that is, the greater
the disorder, the greater the knowledge amount. After analyzing the data over
the 19 research areas, we find that the knowledge amount of most research areas
is increasing over time, and through structural entropy analysis of the
citation network, we find that the knowledge amount of the network is not the
same as the productivity of the entire network, and the productivity of 80% of
the research areas is not equal to the knowledge amount. This research expands
the understanding of scientific productivity and system behavior from the
perspective of knowledge, providing a new tool and new insights for scientific
research policy making and other related decision-making processes.
Moreover, we hope that this study will open up new possibilities for research
on the measurement of knowledge and the evaluation of academic conferences and
journals.
